speechtext:

speechtext:

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce.
Following the announcement of the measures advocated by the minister to control clothing imports, could he advise the House whether he has received representations from importers expressing dissatisfaction over these measures and, on the other hand, whether textiles firms have indicated their support and satisfaction for what has already been done to protect this industry?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: TEXTILES-REACTION OF IMPORTERS AND MANUFACTURERS TO PROTECTIVE MEASURES
speechtext: I shall reply first to the second part of the question, Mr. Speaker. The textile industry and the unions representing textile workers have advised me of their satisfaction about the new policy. On the other hand, importers are faced with a number of problems. Last week, I allowed the entry into Canada of some goods in transit. Concerning other readjustments, I shall try to make the necessary announcements as soon as possible; but we must keep in mind that the government's decision to protect our textile industry is very important now because the import level has reached 50 per cent in 1976, and we have indicated to the importers our intention to maintain imports at the 1975 level.

subtopic: TEXTILES-REACTION OF IMPORTERS AND MANUFACTURERS TO PROTECTIVE MEASURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to ask a supplementary question.
Was the measure announced by the minister taken further to the recommendations of the Textile and Clothing Board which must necessarily report on a regular basis to the minister on this matter, and are these recommendations contained in the last report submitted by this board?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I acted further to the report submitted to me by the Textile and Clothing Board and also with the advice of the Textile Advisory Board which includes representatives of the employers, the union workers and of the governments of Ontario, Manitoba and Quebec.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. As this country had a trade deficit of $10 billion in manufactured goods last year and this is continuing well into this year and getting worse, and as we must greatly increase sales of manufactured products if any significant decrease in unemployment is to take place in this country, is the minister planning to introduce any incentives to induce greater sales efforts abroad for manufactured products, these incentives to be paid in direct proportion to the increased effort that is made? If so, when will the announcement be made?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: INCENTIVES TO INDUCE GREATER SALES EFFORTS ABROAD FOR MANUFACTURED PRODUCTS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I am somewhat surprised to hear of a $10 billion deficit. Last year there was a deficit in our balance of payments under our trades account.
However, this year we have gone back to a surplus position in our trade balance. Naturally, if there are changes in the Income Tax Act they will be announced in a budget brought down by the Minister of Finance and nothing, of course, should be divulged before that time. As for me, Mr. Speaker, I am very eager to foster greater export possibilities. We are taking steps in that direction in many ways. I am in the process of organizing a campaign designed to make our industries aware of the problem and encourage them to get markets abroad. I trust therefore that I shall have everyone's cooperation in that endeavour.

subsubtopic: CHLORINE-USE OF DIAPHRAGM CELL
speechtext: Is the Department of the Environment and/or the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce aware of the SK-Diaccll process developed by the Kureha Chemical Industry Co. Ltd. of Japan, which employs diaphragm cells in the manufacture of chlorine and, if so, what steps have been taken to encourage the adoption of the process by Canadian manufacturers?

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph E. Goodale (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: CHLORINE-USE OF DIAPHRAGM CELL
speechtext:
The Department of the Environment is aware of the SK-Diacell process. The Chlor-Alkali Mercury Regulations published under the Fisheries Act, and the Chlor-Alkali Mercury Emission Standard Regulations to be published under the Clean Air Act, are based on, respectively, best practicable and best available control technology for existing chlor-alkali plants that use the mercury-cell process. To allow for the development of new technology, the control process is not specified in these regulations; individual chlor-alkali plants are left the freedom to comply in their own way. Notwithstanding the chlor-alkali regulations, however, and although no steps have been taken to encourage the adoption of any specific process by chlor-alkali producers, the adoption of processes that use no mercury has, in general, been encouraged. In a letter to chlor-alkali producers, the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment requested that any expansion of existing, or construction of new chlor-alkali plants not result in increased use of the mercury-cell process, and stated that an ultimate goal of this industry should be the elimination of mercury losses to the environment. speakeroldname: Hon. James Hugh Faulkner (for the Prime Minister) moved
speakerposition: Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION (SCIENTIFIC ACTIVITIES) ACT, 1976 MEASURE RESPECTING ORGANIZATION OF CERTAIN SCIENTIFIC ACTIVITIES OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
that Bill C-26, respecting the organization of certain scientific activities of the government of Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to present the bill on government organization concerning scientific activities to the House on behalf of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in whose name the bill stands. The bill is the culmination of a lengthy series of studies, reports, meetings and debates on the subject of science policy as it affects the university sector, the Science Council and certain government laboratories. Before discussing the bill, I first want to congratulate my predecessor, the hon. member for Westmount (Mr. Drury), on the contribution he has made over the past ten years as the minister responsible for the National Research Council, and more recently as science minister, to our understanding of science policy. His vast experience has brought us closer to finding the most productive means of supporting and using science and technology in the national interest.
Let me now make a few remarks on the background to this science policy debate, because it is one which I believe hon. members will wish to keep in mind as they consider this bill. From time to time, governments are faced with problems which are unique in structure and conception and which, accordingly, place particular challenges on policy machinery. Science policy is one such problem. Since "science policy" emerged about ten years ago as an important and identifiable field of concern, Canada has supported a variety of science policy initiatives. I need only remind hon. members of the reports by the OECD, the Science Council, and the Senate committee-so ably chaired by Senator Lamontagne. These and similar publications, and the establishment of my ministry, have created much interest among some countries, particularly those within the OECD, in Canada's efforts to obtain well-balanced policy advice on how science and technology should be supported and used for our national benefit.
Such activity has also touched off within Canada an extensive discussion of goals and objectives for science and technology and of the appropriate mechanisms for achieving them. This discussion has involved scientists inside and outside government, learned societies and professional associations, industry, individual scholars and ministers, academic journals and the public press. The government has studied the reports and followed the dialogue. The debate has explored the role of government in supporting and stimulating science and technology in industry, in universities and in its own laboratories. It has looked at the broad range of ways in which our science

December 13, 1976
Scientific Activities of Government
and technology effort influences, and is influenced by, public policies.
Many recommendations have been made for policy and institutional change. The government has already responded to many of these.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION (SCIENTIFIC ACTIVITIES) ACT, 1976 MEASURE RESPECTING ORGANIZATION OF CERTAIN SCIENTIFIC ACTIVITIES OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Where? Give us an example.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION (SCIENTIFIC ACTIVITIES) ACT, 1976 MEASURE RESPECTING ORGANIZATION OF CERTAIN SCIENTIFIC ACTIVITIES OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
That is precisely what I shall do, if the hon. member will be patient. I would mention, as an example, the Make or Buy policy which was recently extended to cover ongoing research programs, scientific data-gathering and information services in addition to research and development contracts for new programs. During the past three years, research projects totalling some $100 million have been contracted to the private sector. Much of the discussion has, however, centred on the mechanisms for federal support of university research and whether these mechanisms adequately serve the interests of the universities and the country as a whole. It is to that aspect of the national science effort that this bill is mainly directed. I will have more to say at another time about the support of industrial research and research in government laboratories.
The alternatives proposed for university research support have ranged from retention of the present system to a single granting council covering all disciplines. The government has pondered all the options. This bill reflects our carefully considered view, which I shall expand upon in a moment, that in view of future national needs an evolutionary change in the structure of the granting councils is the desirable course in order to create the balance in the support of the different disciplines which will bring the councils' and national objectives into closer harmony. The proposed changes do, I believe, incorporate the best advice the government has received with the least administrative cost and organizational disruption.
Let me, for a moment, further outline the philosophy underlying those parts of the bill dealing with university research support, before getting into its specific provisions. The government has a strong belief in the importance of a healthy and active university research community and I would like to emphasize that point. We recognize, first of all, that research, whether being done in universities or elsewhere, is the process by which new knowledge is created and is really the foundation of all scientific and technological achievement. In universities, the conduct of research by professors, research students and research assistants is important to us for other reasons as well. It adds to the quality of education given to our university students; it also contributes to the training of scientists and scholars who carry their knowledge and their approach to inquiry into all aspects of national life. It is through the support of university research that we have created a base in Canada of highly qualified people and a research capability in many disciplines. Canada must have this capability to ensure that we can tap into the world's output of new knowledge, be able to understand the significance of that knowledge and adapt it to the needs of industry, government and furthering research in the universities. The government must also have

access to advice on complex scientific and technical questions such as nuclear safety and pollutants in our environment. While the universities are not the only source of this advice, they are a most important one.
Canadian universities have accomplished much in research, some of it leading to applications of direct benefit to Canada. Professor Symons said in his recent report to the Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada:
Canada has established a worldwide reputation for leadership in a number of important scientific fields including, for example: fresh water biology research; nuclear physics; physical chemistry; aerial mapping and surveying; the development of geophysical methods and instrumentation; computer science; research into the upper atmosphere; and certain aspects of research in engineering, forestry, agriculture, and the health sciences. University scientists have contributed significantly to the country's achievements and international reputation in such fields.
I would add to that our high level of scholarship and research in certain fields of the social sciences and humanities. As examples, I could point to the publication of the Dictionary of Canadian Biography, and important studies on the special problems of the working environment in the maritimes, juvenile delinquency in Montreal, and the economics of Canada natural resource policy. There are many others.
We have kept very much in mind, during the preparation of this legislation, the environment of continuity and freedom which is required for the fullest exercise of creativity in research. That is why we are fully committed to retain the "peer review" system; we will not jeopardize the expertise and independence with which the councils support, and scholars perform, research. At the same time, we have sought to provide mechanisms by which eminent scholars in the disciplines being supported will oversee the granting process and will advise the government as to how university research may more effectively support national goals. I hasten to add that any approach which seeks arbitrarily to impose specific objectives or priorities on the research community from outside will not be a productive one and will not be instituted.
The government does, however, have a view of the goal the granting councils should pursue. Simply stated, it is "the support of a balanced development of knowledge and of research capability". In working towards this goal, we believe the councils should: (i) encourage excellence in research; (ii) provide a base of advanced knowledge in the universities; (iii) assist in the selective concentration of research activities; (iv) aim for a regional balance in scientific capability; (v) maintain a basic capacity for research training; (vi) encourage curiosity-oriented research; and (vii) encourage research with a potential contribution to national objectives. These are not seven commandments to be adhered to rigidly, but a framework within which to guide growth and evolution of council activities. Like the legislation, these objectives are intended, not as a basis for immediate and radical redirection but to ensure long-term coherence in the federal system of university research granting. The objectives should provide the context for improved communication between the government and the scholarly communities.
December 13, 1976

Now, what is it exactly that this bill provides for in the area of university research granting? First, the bill creates a social sciences and humanities research council. This will leave the Canada Council, which presently supports both the arts and research and scholarly activity in the social sciences and humanities, to focus its attention on the arts and permit the new council on social sciences and humanities to provide support for academic research in these disciplines. This reorganization reflects the growth in size and quality of the social sciences and humanities in this country and the new perception of their importance to the attack on socioeconomic problems, to national sovereignty, and to our cultural development. The Social Science Research Council of Canada and the Humanities Research Council of Canada, which are umbrella organizations for the learned societies, have indicated to me that they are very much behind the creation of this new council.
Second, the bill creates a natural sciences and engineering research council, leaving the National Research Council to give its full attention to the major task of running a large scientific research establishment, industrial research and development support programs, and a national program of scientific and technical information. The creation of the natural sciences and engineering research council recognizes the need for a separate agency to support university research in these disciplines and to foster improved dialogue between natural scientists and research engineers. Canada must remain in the forefront of appropriate areas of basic research and must create an environment in which university investigators will have the fullest opportunity to contribute to the solution of problems of a social, economic, and technological nature. We look to the natural sciences and engineering research council for an imaginative response to such expectations. I would emphasize, here, that the creation of these two new granting councils will require only a minimal increase in administrative costs since the same personnel and office space will be used as at present.
Third, this legislation alters the Medical Research Council Act to remove the restriction preventing its support of research in the public health field. The amendments will permit, in the future, increased involvement by the Medical Research Council in the support of research and training in the area of health care delivery. I need not remind hon. members of the importance of health care delivery to the well-being of Canadians. Other minor changes to the act will facilitate the administration of the council's business.
Before moving to the other parts of this bill, I would like to say a word about the co-ordination of council granting policies and council budgets. It is planned that the division of responsibility for university research support among the councils will be along the same general lines as that which has existed among the Medical Research Council and the university granting programs of the National Research Council and the Canada Council.
I intend to establish, with the cooperation of the new granting bodies, an intercouncil co-ordinating committee chaired by the secretary of the Ministry of State for Science
Scientific Activities of Government and Technology and including the presidents of the granting councils. Other officials will be asked to participate in the work of the committee from time to time, depending on the matters under discussion. The committee will report to me. As its name implies, the committee will have an advisory and co-ordinating role, rather than a directive role. It will be a forum for catalysing collective responses to problems of mutual interest to the granting councils. It will seek to ensure coverage of all recognized disciplines and that the needs of interdisciplinary research are met. It will harmonize granting practices. It will also make recommendations to me on the balance between the budgets of the councils, recognizing, of course, the responsibility of individual ministers for the budget and administration of each council.
It is not anticipated that the intercouncil co-ordinating committee will have a high-visibility public stance but it is certainly my intention that through the councils and by consultations, briefs, hearings or discussions, the academic community will have the opportunity to communicate their views to the committee. I might say here that I will be seeking the views of various groups and individuals in the universities and outside on the membership of the two new councils. We will be aiming for a membership broadly representative of all disciplines being supported and to include, together with the experts, a number of lay people interested in the development of scholarship and scientific research in this country.
I am not unaware of the criticism the government has been receiving about the lack of growth in the council budgets. The present pause in the growth rate, which my predecessor, the hon. member for Westmount, noted many times had followed years of high growth-over 20 per cent per year in the 1960s-has been necessary as a part of the over-all financial restraint in government expenditures. It has caused hardship among university researchers: we recognize this. The competition for limited funds has been tough, and worth-while projects have had to be cut. The government does not want to see the research competence of our universities eroded. The councils together now spend more than $160 million per year on university research, but we know that the costs of that research have been rising because of inflation and the increasing sophistication of scientific equipment. Accordingly, subject to overall fiscal constraints, consideration is being given, in arriving at the councils budgets for 1977-78, to providing appropriate amounts to cover these inflationary increases.
Further, we recognize that while the basis of university research support must continue to be the criterion of excellence, the goal the government has proposed for the councils covers more than this single objective. Therefore, upon passage of the bill I will be requesting additional amounts for council programs relating especially to a regional balance of scientific capability, national problem areas, and the support of interdisciplinary research. The way in which the councils choose to deal with these added objectives is, as I indicated earlier, a matter for the councils to decide. The complexity of many of the problems facing society need new and broadly-based solutions to which university scientists can contribute. I hope that

December 13, 1976
Scientific Activities of Government
the councils will be able, with the additional funds, to more effectively encourage work on unique Canadian problems and develop interdisciplinary initiatives to help our resolution of these problems. I look forward to discussing with the councils the approaches they develop to this new dimension in council activities.
This bill, together with the intercouncil co-ordinating committee and the Canadian committee on financing university research, announced a few weeks ago, should establish a sound administrative framework for the federal granting system. We will not get back to the highly expansionary climate of the late sixties, but I feel confident that this new federal structure will ensure desirable stability and continuity in the years ahead in the government's support of university research. The importance which the universities attach to the federal system of grants for university research has been aptly stated in a paper from the Science Council:
What all must share, whether professors or prime ministers, is a concern for the future intellectual manpower requirements of Canada, which can only be secured by strong, positive, research granting policies. Research grants are essential to high quality university education. Research grants are investments in the future that may also pay short term dividends.
It is the government's intent in the new granting system to have such policies.
Now to the other parts of this bill. Being proposed are amendments to the Science Council Act, the National Research Council Act and the National Defence Act as it affects the Defence Research Board. The Science Council is to have its mandate restated to provide it with a greater national and public role. What do I mean by this? The council has over the years been attempting to prepare all of us to deal intelligently with national issues having important science and technology dimensions. It has commented on the energy question, northern development, health care and university research, among others. We may not agree with all its recommendations but I think, without doubt, the council has brought an enlightened point of view to these issues which has been extremely useful in the realm of both public and private decision-making across the country. The new mandate of the council will state clearly that the council is to act as a source of public information and to provide advice on the profound effects developments in science and technology will continue to have on our way of life. To cope with its broadened responsibilities and to permit the participation of additional social scientists in the work of the council, the membership of the council is to be expanded from 25 to 30.
I have already spoken of the separation of the granting and laboratory functions of the National Research Council. The amendments to the National Research Council Act are designed to give the council flexibility in its management structure so that it can more readily respond to their solution. Provision has also been made to transfer the responsibility for Canadian Patents and Development Limited from the National Research Council to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce in order that the exploitation of inventions from

government laboratories and the university laboratories being supported by the federal government may be linked more closely to the promotion and development of Canadian industry. CPDL will become an even more important vehicle for the transfer of technology from government to industry. Following the publication of the Science Council's report on "Technology Transfer: Government Laboratories to Manufacturing Industry", improved ways are being sought, including new uses of CPDL, to transfer technology from the public to the private sector.
The role of the National Research Council will shift somewhat in emphasis as a result of the proposed changes. The council, without its granting function, will have less responsibility for the general development of science in Canada and more for using the demonstrated capability of its laboratories in tackling national problems. Let me emphasize, however, that there will continue to be room in the council's mandate for the high quality basic research for which it has deservedly attained an international reputation, both for NRC and Canada.
With regard to defence research, the National Defence Act is to be altered to bring the Defence Research Board into organizational integration with its primary customers, the Canadian forces. The board will continue as an advisory group to the Minister of National Defence, while the defence research establishments are consolidated within the department. The legislation serves to clarify the new role of DRB which is already in effect.
This, then, is a general outline of the bill which is before this House, and the background to it. I believe that if the changes recommended are accepted, we can expect science and technology to contribute even more fully than they have in the past to the long-term development of this country.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION (SCIENTIFIC ACTIVITIES) ACT, 1976 MEASURE RESPECTING ORGANIZATION OF CERTAIN SCIENTIFIC ACTIVITIES OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill, as presented, has been around for more than two years. Looking at the state of science and technology in the country today, any suggestion that it would find speedy passage through the House and committee, after two years of marking time, is day-dreaming. When I first heard that the bill was somewhere in the making, I thought it might answer some of the problems we face today in this field. After reading it through, I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that it is about as exciting as watching paint dry. One has to ask at the outset whether this bill is the first step of several which will eliminate the Ministry of State for Science and Technology. It might also be timely to ask why it is being introduced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and not by the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Faulkner). There may be good explanations in answer to these questions, but I feel this is a first step toward dissolution or cancellation of MOSST.
One might really call it a "let's make some jobs for the boys" bill. You may be aware, Mr. Speaker, that the Ministry of State for Science and Technology can be cancelled at any time without reference to parliament: it can be done by order in council. I note that MOSST is not mentioned anywhere in the bill; the legislation states only that the various councils are
December 13, 1976

to report to a minister designated by the governor in council. When we note, too, that the present minister views MOSST as "a policy development ministry providing advice to clients within government" and when we note that the previous minister, the hon. member for Westmount (Mr. Drury), devoted about four hours a week to the ministry, we begin to realize that research and development in the scientific field are low priority items in the government scheme of things.
1 suppose that in the last two years more has been written about science and research than about almost any other subjet. This is a reflection of the continuous decline in research and development funding. Between 1962 and 1967 the gross expenditure on research and development increased from 0.9 per cent of the GNP to 1.4 per cent. In 1972 a Senate committee recommended that national expenditure on research and development should increase to 2.5 per cent in the 1980s. In making this recommendation the Senate committee proposed an inflation rate of 3 per cent.
In spite of this recommendation, the percentage of the GNP allocated to research in 1972 slipped from 1.4 per cent to 1.19 per cent of the GNP. In 1973 we saw a further erosion to 1.12 per cent. The federal government led the way in this reduction. In the mid-sixties it contributed about one-half of the total R and D budget. By the seventies this contribution had shrunk to one-third of the total funds allocated. Couple this with the fact that inflation amounted to more than 10 per cent in 1975, and one begins to realize that the government has no idea what is required. There is no science policy. The supreme insult was delivered in the form of an AIB regulation which classified research and development in the same category as donations to charity, sales promotion and advertising. This regulation, which was withdrawn in the last budget, stated that funds spend on research and development could only be increased if there were a corresponding decrease in sales promotion and advertising or donations to charity.
Where were the strong voices of the ministry and of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce when these regulations were being drafted? MOSST was concentrating on its declared function of being a policy development ministry providing advice to clients within government. We also know that IT and C is in such an administrative muddle, with a giant trade deficit and a multiplicity of alphabet programs, that it was not even aware that the regulations had been put in place by the AIB.
What really does this bill do, Mr. Speaker? Well, it increases the granting councils from four to six. This means six sets of accounting, auditing and administrative people. At a time when the government is talking about restraint in spending, it is increasing its administrative staffs. It would have been much better if these funds had been used for research and development than for administration.
In addition to the six councils to oversee the allocation of grants to the various disciplines, we have the intercouncil co-ordinating committee under the general chairmanship of
Scientific Activities of Government the secretary of MOSST, but ICCC has no budgetary control. This is another layer of bureaucracy and staff inserted in between. It would be much better if the Privy Council, which I understand really drafted this bill, had taken the advice of the Senate committee and set up an over-all Canadian science foundation reporting to a full minister, with a multiplicity of divisions which could deal with the important scientific disciplines. Such a structure could facilitate inter-disciplinary activities; it could utilize common management and financial services, with substantial saving in administrative costs.
The way this bill is structured, Mr. Speaker, each granting council will report to a different minister to be designated by the governor in council. The councils will also report through the intercouncil co-ordinating committee to the secretary of MOSST, and thus to the minister. So, in effect, a council will be reporting to two ministers, if you read the bill and the press release from MOSST. But the bill does not refer to the ICCC in any of its provisions.
Let me look for a moment at some of these councils. I agree that the establishment of the sciences and humanities research council is a good move, but let me examine it in particular and see what is going to happen. It will report to a minister to be designated by the governor in council. The president and vice-president will be appointed by the governor in council or with the approval of the governor in council. It will have 21 other members including the vice-president. The members of the council nominally will be allowed travelling and other expenses while on council business. That is fair enough. Then they may be paid additional remuneration if required for duties assigned to them by the council. I assume members of the executive committee would qualify for the additional remuneration.
Then, because the council is authorized to receive funds, bequests, securities or other property they will have an investment committee consisting of the president, who is appointed by the governor in council, a council member and three other persons appointed by the governor in council. These three persons appointed by the governor in council, not being paid members of the council, can receive remuneration and expenses fixed by the governor in council. The council can have special and standing committees, as well as other committees beyond the executive committee and the investment committee. In addition to the president, vice-president, executive committee, investment committee, special committees and standing committees, the council can establish an advisory committee of persons other than members of the committee. Not being members of the committee, they may be paid remuneration and expenses as fixed by the governor in council.
Further, Mr. Speaker, the council may appoint officers and employees as necessary who in fact are paid salaries and expenses, again approved by the governor in council. In addition to this, the council may appoint persons to perform duties-this is really another way of saying that they will be able to appoint consultants-of a temporary nature.
I think we must take a look at the structure and ask ourselves how much it will all cost, Mr. Speaker. When all

December 13, 1976
Scientific Activities of Government these salaries and expenses are paid to staff, consultants, committees, and so forth, how much money will actually be spent to promote and assist research and scholarships in the social sciences and humanities? In fact, just reading the clause of the bill pertaining to the social sciences and humanities makes me wonder whether there is a better way to do it so that the funds to be allocated to the council can be used to better advantage. It begs the question: Will the people of Canada be well served? Will their tax dollars be properly spent or, as I have said, are we just making some jobs for the boys?
The function of the natural sciences and engineering research council is somewhat similar to the social sciences and humanities research council except that it does not have an investment committee. It is rather strange that the meaning of the title is not carried through in the functions to be performed by the council. In other words, there is no engineering function to be carried out; it merely describes the function of the natural sciences and engineering research council, which is "to promote and assist research in the natural sciences other than health sciences". It will also advise the minister, who has not been designated, on the matters he may refer to the council for its consideration. Again, it is rather fuzzy. A lot of people without too much direction as to function will be reporting to an unknown minister on projects to be assigned to them by another unknown minister.
The Science Council of Canada is stripped of most of its former duties as set forth in section 11 of the original act. It will now be required to assess the technological resources, requirements and potentialities of Canada and increase the public awareness of scientific and technological problems and opportunities. In other words, the Science Council of Canada will become a science and technology public relations corporation. It assesses potential and increases public awareness. I think this is a shame. I have always held the Science Council of Canada in very high regard and I think this is quite a comedown for the council.
The National Research Council, according to the bill, loses its granting function. It loses Canadian Patents and Development Limited and will now have charge of all matters affecting scientific and industrial research in Canada which may be assigned to it by the governor in council. Previously its duties were assigned to it by a committee. In short, the National Research Council now operates only laboratories and carries out research as directed by the governor in council. We can see from the addition of a new section that the council can undertake to spend moneys received by the council through its operations. We will want some explanations for this item, as it may run afoul of the Auditor General. I think we should try and head that off at the beginning. If I read that particular section correctly, it will be in conflict with the Auditor General. I agree that the National Research Council should be able to use any funds it receives for contracting work that it does to help offset its overhead, but by the same token clause 59(2)(e) of the bill provides:
(e) to expend, for the purposes of this act, any money appropriated by parliament for the work of the council or received by the council through the conduct of its operations-

We have had instances of that in the past. The Auditor General has always taken the position that funds so received should go to the general revenue fund. We would want to find some other mechanism and see whether we can arrange it in such a way that this will not be in conflict with the Auditor General.
The Defence Research Board change is merely an administrative clean-up. I understand the changes recommended have already been made, but we must question what has happened to the research facilities of the Defence Industrial Research Board. The minister stated in his remarks that this had been incorporated into the department. As I recall, it has a budget of $5 million and certain facilities. What is happening to these facilities today? These are the things we will want to discuss when this matter comes before the committee.
The transfer of Canadian Patents and Development Limited to Industry, Trade and Commerce is a logical move. However, I think we will want to hear from the minister just what he plans to do with this corporation. We want to be sure that it is not lost in the administrative gazebo of Industry, Trade and Commerce. This organization has a tremendous potential for transferring known technology to industry. Recent studies on productivity have indicated there is a tremendous lag in the transfer or the utilization of known technology in our secondary industries. It might be wise to consider retaining Canadian Patents and Development Limited as a full agency corporation. I think it has a very important role to play, and I would be very upset if we found, in fact, that Canadian Patents and Development Limited was shuffled off into a corner of Industry, Trade and Commerce and lost in the administrative mess we see in that department.
The information document released with Bill C-26 implies that there has been broad consultation and discussion with the scientific and research communities on the structure of this bill. We know in fact there was not. While there may have been discussions within the departments with a few select people, there has been little discussion outside government offices. In fact, it has been suggested-and I was rather surprised and shocked when I heard this-that the Minister of State for Science and Technology may have conveyed to some people in the research community that they should not oppose the recommendations in this bill. In other words: don't rock the boat, or else. Remember the sad state of research and-

speechtext:
If the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. MacFarlane) wants to get into this debate, he should put his name on the list. Remembering the sad state of research, the lack of firm science policy and the bland promises by the minister that he would be requesting additional funds for a council program to compensate for inflation, we have to say that this really is not such a program. We can see few
December 13, 1976

remedies in the proposed bill. In fact, by the time the expanded councils are staffed, I think we could have a net decrease in existing levels of research funding.
In many of our government research laboratories we find that the research staff is quite upset. The staff is required to reduce its operating budget to pay for salary increases. In other words, the top limit must be adhered to regardless of the research being carried on. If this regulation were carried to its conclusion, it would totally eliminate the operating budget or drastically reduce the amount of research that can be undertaken. One can only conclude that it would have been much better for Canada had the additional $100 million being allocated for LIP grants been channelled into research at all levels.
The state of industrial research in this country is at a very low ebb. Consider these facts. We have a balance of payments deficit for manufactured goods of $10 billion. In addition, 80 per cent of manufactured products in Canada are made by companies with less than 50 employees. Taking all the research carried on by companies in the private sector, and noting the number of researchers, the average is two per company and the bulk are in large corporations. Then considering that there is a low level of transfer of technology to small and medium-sized companies in Canada, the companies which produce 80 per cent of the goods manufactured in Canada, one would have to say that this bill certainly does not address itself to the problems.
Consider, as well, the proposed patent law legislation put forth by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Abbott). When putting the two together, one has to ask where all the misdirection is leading us. There is no co-ordination, plan or policy, but just a series of disjointed, unrelated moves that in total spell, to my mind, disaster to research and development in the private sector.
We know that the United States government is funding a national centre for corporate technology. A similar move has been made in Europe. We find, of course, that Japan has been a leader in this particular process. There is no recognition of this or the need for it, in spite of overwhelming evidence that such a structure is required. This bill, in fact, has so many flaws and weaknesses that we feel strongly we should have a series of intensive committee, hearings with witnesses from the academic community, from various scientific disciplines, including the engineering community, the small business sector and industry, so they may place their views before the committee in order that they may become part of the restructuring of scientific and industrial research in Canada.
I could go on, as the Chair has informed me I have unlimited time, but I think I have covered the major points 1 wanted to make. Of course, I will have more to say about the restructuring of scientific and industrial research in the committee. Just let me say I am very disappointed that this bill does not come to the central point we have been dealing with here. I am disappointed in the minister. He is a new minister, and I thought he might have been a little more gung-ho in looking at the problems facing the country, really getting with
Scientific Activities of Government them. As I read this bill, it is a shuffling of chairs and furniture. It is inserting another layer of bureaucracy into the system, and I really do not think it is going to solve the problems facing the country. We have some serious problems to be dealt with in research.
This afternoon my colleague asked the minister a question about coal gasification. Given the deposits we have in this country, and looking at the state of energy costs in the maritimes, one would think we would be a leader in this process. But, in fact, all I can find out about what is going on in that regard is that somebody is looking at it and some research is being carried on in the maritimes as to how to get excess levels of sulphur out of the coal so that we can perhaps make better use of it in some of our processes.
There are many other things to be considered. The spruce budworm problem in the maritimes has been with us for a number of years. In fact, if that is not dealt with severely in the very near future we may not have a forest to any extent in New Brunswick a few years down the road. So we can go, right across the country. We find that the medical research people have made their presence felt in Ottawa and have put forth a very strong lobby for their case. I have a great deal of understanding for their problems, and my colleague will be dealing with them as the debate continues. We can look at the problems that are facing us right across this country in technology and research development, whether it be at the university level or at the industrial level. There is nothing in this bill, as I see it, that deals with it, and I feel very regretful that having this opportunity to do something, nothing is being done. I hope that when the bill eventually goes to committee, whenever that may be, we can have extensive hearings, have people come here from various disciplines and, if possible, restructure the bill so that it will answer the problems facing Canada today.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION (SCIENTIFIC ACTIVITIES) ACT, 1976 MEASURE RESPECTING ORGANIZATION OF CERTAIN SCIENTIFIC ACTIVITIES OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to make a few comments on Bill C-26 to reorganize the granting councils. I apologize for the absence of my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), who intended to speak on this bill but had a prior commitment in his riding.
The Bill before us proposes to reorganize the granting councils of Canada from the present three we have to five other major ones. We have the National Research Council, the Medical Research Council, and the Canada Council. They will be reorganized into the National Research Council, which will look after laboratories but will not have a granding function, the Canada Council which will support the arts, the Medical Research Council which will support research into health sciences, a new council called the natural sciences and engineering research council, which will support research in those fields, and another new council, the social sciences and humanities research council, which will support research in those fields.

December 13, 1976
Scientific Activities of Government
I was intrigued by the timing of this bill. It appears to me that whenever the Liberal government gets into trouble and has no real policy answers or a commitment to change things, it carries out the old double-shuffle; it reorganizes parts of its bureaucracy with great fanfare to make it appear that it is doing something, whereas in actuality it is just shuffling the cards and not changing anything. I think, for example, of the time in the past when they split unemployment insurance and the manpower departments, saying that this was a more efficient way of handling the manpower and unemployment policies. Then, in the intervening years, unemployment continued to increase, manpower was not successful in placing people, and there were abuses in the unemployment insurance program. So, with great fanfare, they came out with a new policy rejoining the two departments and it appeared that something of substance was being done, but we know otherwise. So I am rather suspicious when we think of the timing of this bill, because in the past few years what has been happening to the scientific and research community in Canada has been a shocking decrease in the funding in these important areas in our universities and elsewhere.
More recently, under the government's restraint program the freeze and cutbacks in the research grants have been even more telling. During the past year we witnessed a very intense lobby on Parliament Hill by the scientific and research communities who were very much alarmed at what was happening to their disciplines. Certainly we in this party share their concern. I still think, however, that despite that lobby the government will not come forward with adequate funding. So 1 am suspicious that this bill, as we see it today, is a sop to that lobbying effort and an attempt to make it appear that the government is interested in science and research and that it is doing something, but really what we see here is a reorganization of some of the councils but no commitment on the part of the government to maintain adequate funding.
I could support the concept of reorganization if we had some kind of iron-clad guarantee that this government was serious about funding, but we do not have that as yet. So I should like to develop that theme in my speech to try to illustrate the severity of the problem and to impress upon the government that, in addition to the reorganization of the councils, there must be a rethinking of funding for the councils and of the important activities supported by it. In the first area of science and scientific research and development, I think all hon. members, at least in the opposition parties, recognize the importance of scientific research and adequate funding.
We in Canada are confronted with many problems in resource management and energy development. I think of the new technology in the oil sands and the need to explore alternative energy to fossil fuels, such as sun and wind power, and the need for research in these areas. I think of the problems of food supply, climate and soil and how we need research in these areas. In my area of northern Ontario, forest management is a very important field and certainly diseases in the forest, such as the spruce budworm plague and other kinds of diseases, are very significant factors in the economy of an

area such as northern Ontario. We have not had enough scientific investigation into pollution problems which are unique or of prominence in Canada in terms of our industrial development. We could go on with new development in transportation, rapid transit and communications in this vast country, satellite communications and otherwise.
In all these areas we certainly recognize the need for adequate research, yet when we look at the budgeting and the kinds of programs that are now underway we find serious gaps in them. I reject outright the proposition put forward by the former minister of science and technology, now the hon. member for Westmount (Mr. Drury), that we can rely on foreign technology and research, that we can import this research, and that we do not have to put a priority on the development of Canadian research and scientific experiment.
I do not believe-and I do not think anyone in the scientific community in Canada believes-that we can rely on other countries to address themselves to problems facing Canadians, and that we can borrow their development, their research and new discoveries. 1 think, for example, of problems in northern Ontario such as mercury pollution into which we should have had some energetic investigation many years ago, instead of relying on the Swedes and the Japanese to come forward with scientific information. Mercury pollution is certainly affecting many Indian communities in northwestern Ontario and Quebec. So I reject the idea of the hon. member for West-mount that we can import our research and development. Intellectually, that would put us into a colonial status regarding research, which is totally unacceptable for a modern, industrialized country such as Canada. We cannot afford to waste the talent of our students in universities who, because of the absence of this government's commitment to science and research, in many cases are unable to pursue research in their special fields even during their university years, let alone after they graduate. We have seen far too many of our young university graduates-and we, as taxpayers, put money into university education-having to move to the United States to be employed in their respective fields of endeavour because Canada has not committed itself to such research. I think there is talent here in Canada, but we need funds so that we can develop sophisticated technology and so that we do not have to import it. We need funds so that Canadians in these very important fields-graduates, technicians and others-do not have to join unemployment lines or move out of the country.
So we can agree on the necessity of a vigorous, well funded science and research program. But what has been the record to date of the Liberal government in this field? I think the point can be made by looking at two aspects of this government's policy, or lack of it. First, I notice a lack of direction and, second, a lack of funding. The Senate committee which did a very thorough investigation of science policy in Canada defined science policy as, "The planned use of science in support of national goals." The words "national goals" are key here, because if we are going to help scientists and other
December 13, 1976

researchers it should be done within the framework of some national goals and some knowledge of where we are going as a country in various fields.
What are the goals of the federal government? Rather than goals, we see ad hoc reactions to situations or crises as they may come up. Where is an industrial strategy for Canada which will get us out of the bind of always relying on exporting our natural resources and, hence, getting into the dilemma of not having job-intensive manufacturing industries here, and as a result, high unemployment? Where is an industrial strategy to get more manufacturing industries to provide not only for researchers but also for general labourers?
Where is the industrial strategy to end the kind of stranglehold we have experienced as a result of being a branch plant economy? The branch plants in Canada are controlled by parent companies, usually in the United States, and 60 per cent of our manufacturing industries are foreign-owned. Research and development is carried out in the parent plants; they do not delegate it to the branch plants here in Canada. So if we have a goal of repatriating the Canadian economy, that would fit in with a goal of scientific development in terms of technology for manufacturing.
What is the goal of this government with regard to health care? Recently this parliament passed Bill C-68 to cut back funding commitments for medicare. That bill reversed a direction I thought this country was taking in terms of preserving universal health and medical care. What are the goals for housing and for a national education policy in co-operation with the provinces? What I am saying is that we will continue to lack direction unless this government gets serious about national goals. In many cases we see lack of direction in our science policies as well. However, the key area where there is lack of leadership is in funding. Anyone who looks at the record of the federal government over the past few years regarding funding of science and research cannot help but be shocked at the decline in funding in Canadian industry, in government laboratories and also in universities.
With regard to research and development in industry in relation to the gross national product, by 1975 the funds committed to industrial research were only 87 per cent of the level of 1969. For example, the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce abolished its IRDIA program which amounted to some $32 million in fiscal year 1974-75. This was a program to back research. The department has also cut back its PAIT program. The effects of the cutbacks in these two programs have hampered attempts to improve foreign markets and technology, both of which are related to science research. In terms of our branch plant economy, which I mentioned earlier, we can see the results of the lack of development when we compare Canada with other countries. For example, in France, West Germany, Japan, The Netherlands and Sweden, research and development manpower engaged in industry on the average is about 25 people per 10,000 population; but in Canada it is only about 8 people per 10,000. That, again, is a shocking state of affairs in a country which is supposedly industrialized and well developed.
Scientific Activities of Government
We can also see the effects of cutbacks in funding at government laboratories. The level of funding for 1975-76 is only 83 per cent of that of 1969 in relation to the gross national product. In real terms there is a decline in what the dollar can buy for those research laboratories, compared with a few years ago. To illustrate what I mean by that, we find that between 1969 and 1974 the funding for the National Research Council increased by 6.2 per cent, but in the same period of time the consumer price index rose by over 24 per cent. To quote a few statistics which will illustrate what is happening, the cost of laboratory supplies and equipment rose by over 16 per cent during that period; glassware was up 21 per cent; organic chemicals rose in cost by anywhere from 30 per cent to 400 per cent; yet in its budget the government uses a common figure of 5 per cent as an over-all measure of cost increases. That is just unrelated to the actualities of the situation.
Research funding for universities has declined as well. The level of funding for science and engineering by 1975 was reduced to 67 per cent of the 1969 level. We found that the freezing of grants for 1976 brought the decline to an even lower figure of 60 per cent. When we think of the rising enrolment in some scientific fields and the demands on scientific budgets in universities, surely this is an intolerable situation. Yet we see a corresponding cut because of inflation. I can best sum it up by quoting from the brief submitted to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on March 12, 1976, by the Royal Society of Canada. I think these experts in the field put the matter in perspective when they said, at page 2 of the brief:
Freezes and actual cutbacks in current dollars, together with inflation have so impoverished R and D in the three sectors that today we are facing the break-up of competent research groups that took many years to establish, the downgrading of the quality and scope of research, and some loss of morale among researchers. These consequences are in addition to the serious damage that has been done to the potential contributions of scientific R and D to the Canadian economy.
The evidence is there, Mr. Speaker. This government has deliberately allowed funding to decline to the point that our scientific community is very worried about the continued state of this important profession in the future of Canada. The trend is much the same in the social sciences. Until now they have been funded by the Canada Council and the federal government. Social sciences and humanities research have been neglected to the point of crisis. Some modest increases in funding have been made in the past, but they still do not meet the needs of this country.
We cannot rely on social sciences in other countries to do the investigations that we need so desperately here. We cannot rely on American or Italian social scientists to analyse what is happening in Quebec in terms of separation. We need Canadians to investigate this area and to put on paper the pros and cons of an independent Quebec vis-a-vis Canada in terms of economic survival, etc. That research has not been done in Canada because we do not have enough funding. There is need for more research on social welfare and how it affects the
1946

December 13, 1976
Scientific Activities of Government
regions of Canada and the policies of this government. We cannot rely on foreign social scientists to do that.
On March 4, 1976, the Social Science Research Council of Canada presented a brief to the government outlining the problems faced by social scientists in this country. Anyone who reads that brief must worry about the state of the social sciences in Canada and the lack of research. On page 3, the brief points out:
Human science research and development performed by universities for the federal government has declined from 51.4 per cent of the federal extramural R and D dollar in 1971-72 to 34.7 per cent in 1975-76.
The brief concludes that the universities have not maintained their relative role as performers of extramural R and D in the human sciences and have not benefitted from the slight improvement made in the past. When you examined the role of the Canada Council in funding social scientists, it can be seen that there are areas of concern there as well. On page 4 of the same report we read:
If the Canada Council is the main supplier of funds for basic research in the humanities and social sciences and if the universities are the main performers of such research, basic research in the humanities and social sciences is in an even worse condition in 1976 than it was in 1972 when the Senate committee's recommendations were published. If, in addition, the annual rate of inflation is taken into account, the modest over-all gains did not even maintain levels of support and the Canada Council and the universities, and hence the community of humanities and social science scholars, have lost more ground relative to other suppliers and performers in the human science field.
In this field, as well, we see the problem of lack of funding and lack of serious commitment on the part of the government. The Canada Council is going to be affected by this bill. In 1975 the council gave over $24 million to the social sciences and humanities and over $23 million to the arts. In passing, Mr. Speaker, I should like to note with some concern the rumour that in the 1977 budget Treasury Board is not going to increase the allotments to the Canada Council that would make up for increasing costs and inflation.
I have received, as I am sure other members of parliament have, representations from many artistic groups concerned about what will be happening to Canada Council funding next year. Symphony orchestras, for example, are concerned that the limits will mean they cannot operate, and this is certainly true of the symphony at Sault Ste. Marie, as well as those in smaller communities. Canada Council funds available for grants and scholarships were up 26 per cent in current dollars in the period 1969 to 1975, but in terms of real dollars, when you take into account the inflation rate, that has declined by 5 per cent. So the real dollars have not been forthcoming.
The Medical Research Council is also faced with problems. We all recognize the importance of research in medicine, pharmacy and dentistry, not only for prevention but also for the treatment of disease. Last spring the government announced a freeze on research grants and the council had to cancel its June grant competition. Many skilled technicians in the medical field did not receive a salary increase and others were laid off. At the University of Manitoba the medical faculty had to reduce the number of technicians from 15 to 8. There was, again, total lack of comprehension on the part of

the government of the need for adequate medical research funding.
A letter I received from the Lady Davis Institute for Medical Research dated May 14, 1976, sums up the situation when it says:
With all the government's valid concern about strengthening the Canadian identity, there appear to be certain cabinet ministers who are unable to comprehend the advantages to Canada of strengthening its involvement not only in commerce and the arts, but in the sciences, including medical science, as well. They are reportedly content to "import" the benefits of medical research done elsewhere; in view of the wealth of this country, such a parasitic attitude is reprehensible. Of greater importance, these ministers fail to understand that the existence of a strong research program is an essential component in the development and sustenance of the coterie of physicians and medical scientists whose concern, curiosity and intellectual drive make them the leaders of the medical community. These are the men and women who evaluate and introduce new concepts and methods, who stimulate and teach both the practitioners of today and the medical students who will be the physicians of tomorrow. These are the men and women whose presence makes the difference in our community between good medical care and excellent medical care.
I have tried to illustrate, with examples relating to disciplines over which granting councils have authority, that the government is not concerned about funding. The bill before the House seeks to restructure the granting councils and, hence, the way funds are distributed. I, and I think most in the scientific community, welcome that proposed change but say that restructuring without adequate funding is nothing but a charade, a put-on. In my opinion, the government must give an iron-clad minimum commitment that it will not allow the level of funding to fall behind because of inflation. It must also commit itself to a long-range funding program so that on the basis of clearly stated goals, about which we have not heard so far, the scientific community can plan with confidence what is necessary, instead of worrying from year to year that a program will be cut off halfway through its life because of lack of funding. We must make a funding commitment with regard to research and science policy if the restructuring of the granting councils is to be meaningful.
We must scrutinize carefully the make-up of these granting councils. I shall say more about this in committee. We must make sure that people highly knowledgeable and qualified in their fields are appointed to these granting councils and that various interest groups as well as individuals have representation on such councils. Perhaps we ought to adhere to the formula of appointing two-thirds of the members from the academic, scientific and technical community and one-third from the public at large, which should include representatives of labour, the professions and other interest groups.
We must consider carefully the process by which members are appointed to such granting councils. The process should be much more open. Nominations should be submitted by a variety of interest groups. In other words, the number of groups submitting possible nominations to these councils should be as large as possible. Although the regional balance is important, I would not want to see the formula so rigidly applied as to deny highly skilled people the opportunity to
December 13, 1976

serve, particularly, say, in cases where an academic might be transferred to another part of the country.
I shall also want to ask questions about the allocation of grants. I suspect that in some cases there is a bias, perhaps even favouritism, in granting procedures. This is especially true in the arts. It is important to consider smaller artistic groups in the more remote regions of the country, in addition to the more notable artistic groups. These remarks also apply to individuals engaged in the arts and to those in the scientific community.
I am concerned in case bureaucrats in the appropriate ministries exercise undue influence on the funding recommendations of the various councils. We must watch this closely. We must make certain that advisory groups in research and science wield real influence and are not mere rubber-stamps in the eyes of the bureaucracy. I think the proposed intercouncil co-ordinating committee chaired by the Secretary of the Ministry of State for Science and Technology will need to be closely scrutinized. I want to know where the real power will lie. Will it be with the bureaucracy, or with the councils to be set up?
As I said in my opening remarks, I am worried because, although the government may give the appearance of acting in science and research policy by shuffling around the councils, in reality it will do very little unless it makes a serious funding commitment. Therefore, I and others who will speak in committee will seek assurances from the government that it will give a commitment for adequate funding in this vitally important field. As far as I am concerned, the bill shows no real change of attitude on the part of the government to science policy, especially in funding.
I want to see real advances forthcoming in the area of funding and I hope the minister and his cabinet colleagues will give us the necessary assurances. Otherwise we shall have created a new level of bureaucracy while the research and scientific activities in this country will continue to wither. I do not want to see this country becoming a colony again in relying on others to do its research and development work. While I support in principle the reorganization proposed by the bill, I say that unless such reorganization is accompanied with a new and larger commitment for funding, the scientific and research fields of this country will not be well served.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION (SCIENTIFIC ACTIVITIES) ACT, 1976 MEASURE RESPECTING ORGANIZATION OF CERTAIN SCIENTIFIC ACTIVITIES OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have awaited this day with great anticipation, because I knew that today the newly appointed Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Faulkner) would make his first speech in his new capacity in this House. I cannot help saying that as 1 listened to him I experienced a sinking feeling. A few days ago, when I asked him in the House if he would follow the same general policy in science as his predecessor, the hon. member for Westmount (Mr. Drury), the minister did not have the courage to respond. He simply sat there, as he is now sitting. I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) the same question and he, too, refused to reply.
Scientific Activities of Government
Today the minister provided some answers. We learned that the policy will remain the same, which means that there is to be no policy and that the government proposes to import scientific and technological knowledge from other countries. I am sorry the minister chose to waste the present opportunity. Instead of telling us something useful in terms of new policy directions, he put on a flim-flam show in typical Liberal fashion and announced he would make changes simply for the sake of change, without considering whether those changes will be useful for the country. While I will not make any firm commitment with regard to my position on the bill at this time, it is my first impression that this bill will not change significantly the science policy of this country. That policy will not change so long as the government opposite continues in power. The minister indicated that somehow he envisages these new councils and the newly proposed committee as lending stability and continuity to the government's support of university research. Frankly, I was confused when he said that, because from the viewpoint of the scientific community previous government programs have not led to stability. Yet, the minister suggested that there would be continuity of previous stability. If that is what he meant, if this new proposal will lead to the sort of stability which the scientific community experienced in the past, I can only say that I view with grave reservations what is to happen to this country's scientific community.
Based on its experience of the past couple of years, the scientific community feels that the government's policies have led to the opposite of stability. There has been little stability in funding and in the security of jobs in the general research field. We know that many ongoing research projects connected with all aspects of science have been cancelled. When we look at the make-up of the research community, we see that it is an aging population. That is largely a result of this government's action. I am not saying that they are all aged. However, the effect is that very few young people in this country are choosing scientific research as a career. They would be foolish to do so under the kinds of policies this government has been following.
We know that it takes a long time to train a researcher. Some have suggested it takes 12 years and perhaps more. If a researcher cannot be assured of a job upon completion of this training and, beyond that, if he cannot be assured of stable employment in this country for the rest of his career, why should he invest so many years of his life training himself just to come to the end of the training period and find that he has to drive a taxi or do some other job for which he was not trained? That is the very thing that is now happening in our scientific community.
Many researchers whose funding has been cut off found themselves in a position where they had to go to other countries to find employment which is in keeping with their training. Many have found it necessary to change careers. Indeed, they face the very painful prospect of having invested in years of training and now having to look for something else to do. Some have already done that. There are examples of MDs who

Yes, some come into politics and participate in the debates in this House. In my view, there are not enough of them here. If I can say anything to the research community, that might be one suggestion that will enable them to speak a little more forcibly and forcefully in terms of protection of science in this country.
If this government continues any longer with its policies, there will be another bird added to the endangered species list-science and the scientists in this country, I was hoping that the minister, who just recently took this job, would reassure me sufficiently that the scientist is not a vanishing breed. Unfortunately, he did not give me any reassurance along those lines.
The minister said there was going to be more stability in the scientific field as a result of this bill. However, he did not say how that will be achieved. He participated in a long harangue of vague generalities. The longer I listen to this debate, the more I think there will be less money for research after this bill passes, and I presume it will by virtue of the government majority. It may take a while to do so, but it will probably pass eventually.
We have a situation where the minister is not explaining how this legislation will benefit the country. Indeed, we are establishing a few new layers of administrative bureaucracy. Looking at the dollars available to the research area in general, what we have here is a redistribution of those dollars with the greater percentage going into administrative bodies and less going into the research field. The minister made some comment about budgeting. He said that for 1976-77 or 197778-in any event, the next year for which budgets will be allocated-there is going to be an increase at least in keeping with inflation. He did not say whether that would just catch up with the inflation of the past year, or of the past four or five years where the various funding agencies have not kept up with inflation.
I am a little nervous about the intercouncil co-ordinating committee. That is because there does not appear to be any input into this committee from the scientific community itself. The chairman is going to be a bureaucrat directly answerable to the minister. If one wanted" to be suspicious, one might construe this to be the first step by this government in an endeavour to place total and complete control over scientific research in this country, undermining the traditional academic freedom which scientists have enjoyed thus far.
If the minister is listening to what I am saying, I would suggest to him that he reconsider the position of chairman of the intercouncil co-ordinating committee and appoint a scientist who is directly engaged in scientific research. There are many good reasons for that. The primary one is that the individual would know the problem; he is most closely connect-

ed to the scientific community and he would be most suited to chair such a committee.
