speechtext:
My colleague suggests that after the next election we will appoint a member from the other side. That is a question on which we shall have to defer a decision for the time being. I can think of no good reason for the minister wanting one of his bureaucrats chairing the intercouncil coordinating committee, unless he thinks he can control the actions of that committee better if one of his underlings is in charge of it. The rest of the members of the committee will be bureaucrats, as well. I am not saying they should all be changed, but perhaps that is another thought one should consider. The chairman should certainly be changed. I do not want to sound as though I am reflecting on a particular individual because I, personally, do not know the bureaucrat involved here: I do not know his name or what he is doing at the moment. Suffice it to say I would rather see an active scientist taking this position. It would be of greater benefit to the scientific community in general.
I was interested in and concerned about the fact that the minister chose to use some, perhaps not forceful but at least some pressure tactics on the scientific community not to object to this legislation. He did not state during his comments why he did that, whether he had something to hide or whether it was part of his apparent desire to speed this bill through the House with virtually no debate. My impression is that the minister thought the bill would get through the House today with minimal debate. Every time a minister wants to sneak something through the House very quickly, I immediately start to wonder why. Perhaps if we can keep this going for a long time, we will get some answers as to why the minister is in such a big hurry, particularly when the bill has been lying around for a couple of years and could have been considered in the past.
I have already stated that nowhere in this bill, nor in the minister's speech, has it been outlined what this government's science policy is or is going to be. The minister totally neglected this very important area. It is important that we know, and it is important that the scientific community know.
We have some facts that we know. One is that Canada is very far behind in its funding policies for scientific research. We are somewhere at about 40 per cent of the level of funding of other western developed nations in so far as general scientific research is concerned. We are funding much less than that on a per capita basis, in terms of medical research. If the minister wants to make a useful contribution to this debate, he will tell us that Canada will take steps at least to catch up to other countries of the western industrialized world in terms of our commitment of funding to research. That is not to say we are not doing good work in some areas. I think we are. Everyone acknowledges that Canada has many good scientists and that we are doing many good works. But when we compare our commitment by way of funding to that of other
December 13, 1976

nations in the developed world, we have to admit we are far behind and should be taking corrective action to ensure that we do not remain far behind for very long. If we, as a nation, want to have a great future, we must see that the scientific community flourishes.
I was most concerned, when I held some meetings with representatives of the Canada's Research Organizations, to find a strong feeling existing among them that we were adopting a "banana republic" attitude toward scientific research, taking the attitude that it was not particularly beneficial to us as a nation and scarcely worth undertaking. Indeed, it does appear as though the government is basing its policies on political expendiency, and even from that point of view its actions are shortsighted: it is still more sensible to spend money on scientific research, because the more we invest now, the more the nation will save in the future. To take the field of industrial research alone, the more we invest in research, the greater will be the profits in the long run.
The minister told us, somewhat apologetically, that funding has been somewhat low in the past couple of years, and the reason he suggested was the existence of the restraint program. Well, Mr. Speaker, if that is the reason, I am afraid I cannot accept it. All we need to do is look at the Auditor General's report and compare the hundreds of millions of dollars totally wasted with the $160 million total budget for all the scientific research to which the government is committed.
In a situation like this, it is altogether illogical to say that cutting the research budget is exercising restraint. It seems more logical to insist that the areas to be attacked should be the areas to which the Auditor General drew attention in his report. I should like to hear the minister explain why he is agreeing with his colleagues to pay so little attention to the claims of scientific research when an opportunity so plainly exists to put an end to wasteful expenditures of the kind to which the Auditor General referred. In my view, a grea t deal more effort could be made to show restraint in that area, and the funds so saved could be channelled into research of one kind or another.
Bill C-26 increases the number of councils from four to six and four of these will be directly engaged in providing research grants. In the case of the National Research Council, the segregation of the granting function from laboratory operations seems reasonably and in accordance with the recommendations of the Macdonald report. This will enable NRC to concentrate on its primary function of performing research in support of industrial needs and encourage a shift in emphasis from basic to applied research.
However, while there is a superficial rationale for the segregation of the granting function by scientific fields, the proliferation of administering agencies would appear to be neither effective nor efficient. As an alternative, consideration should be given to the possibility of an integrated granting agency as represented by the U.S. National Science Foundation. The NSF model offers the advantage of a multiplicity of divisions
Adjournment Motion
dealing individually with the important scientific disciplines and at the same time facilitating interdisciplinary activities. It also utilizes common management and financial services with substantial savings in administrative costs.
This legislation apparently provides for each of the granting councils to report to a different "designated minister". As a corollary, the funding requirements of the individual councils will have to be considered in isolation within the different departmental budgets. For reasons I shall outline, this will create problems with co-ordination and priorities. On these grounds, the Senate committee recommended that a single minister, the Secretary of State, carry responsibility for all of the research councils. In the U.K. this responsibility is borne by the minister of education and science. The ambiguity of Bill C-26 on this score raises the obvious question as to why this responsibility has not been assigned to the Minister of State for Science and Technology, who otherwise has no legislative status or function.
With the multiplicity of granting councils involved, a very real problem will occur in ensuring consistency of policies and operating practices in the awarding of grants. An equally critical problem will arise in determining the allocation of grant funds between the competing claims of the several councils. In other words, Bill C-26 does not provide for the central direction of university research grants envisaged in the report of the Senate committee. In the United Kingdom, where a similar pattern of research activities exist, this function is performed by an advisory board.

subsubtopic: TASK FORCE TO REVIEW PUBLIC SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of establishing a special task force to review the Public Service Employment Act and the role of the commission in personnel management and employer-employee relations in the public service and that the review include an examination of the role assigned the Public Service Commission and its relationship to the Treasury Board Secretariat and the Public Staff Relations Board; and
That the review entail a study of the relationship of the Public Service Commission and the departments and agencies; and consider the development of an audit system for performance accountability with respect to matters delegated to departments and agencies under the Public Service Employment Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, on April 18, 1973, the then president of the privy council wrote to Mr. Jacob Finkelman, Q.C., who was chairman of the Public Service Staff Relations Board, asking him to examine the Public Service Staff Relations Act and its administration and to make recommendations as to how the act should be amended or reviewed. The terms of reference given to Mr. Finkelman did not mention the Public Service Employment Act, though the letter from the then president of the privy council states that Mr. Finkelman was not precluded from making recommendations with respect to those sections of the Public Service Employment Act which were affected by recommendations which may be made regarding the Public Service Staff Relations Act.
The three-volume document prepared by Mr. Jacob Finkelman, Q.C., is dated March, 1974. in accordance with an order of reference of the House of Commons of Tuesday, October 22, 1974, and of the Senate of October 23, 1974, a special joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons considered Parts I, II, and III of the documents entitled "Employer-Employee Relations in the Public Service of Canada". This joint committee was duly organized on November 13, 1974. Thirty-one briefs were received and considered. Witnesses from 19 groups appeared before the committee until July of 1975, after which the committee continued evaluation of the evidence. On Thursday, February 26 of this year, I tabled in this House, in my capacity as joint chairman, the
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Turner).]
sixth and final report of the Special Joint Committee on Employer-Employee Relations in the Public Service.
Motion No. 19 which is now before us is composed of the first three recommendations of the special joint committee. It calls for the establishment of a special task force to review the Public Service Employment Act. The task force would also look at the role of the Public Service Commission in personnel management. The major responsibility under the Public Service Employment Act of staffing, including recruitment, selection, appointment and appeal, was entrusted to the Public Service Commission. The Public Service Commission derives its authority and responsibility from the Public Service Employment Act.
On December 4, 1974, Mr. Carson, chairman of the Public Service Commission, had urged the special joint committee to review the entire Public Service Employment Act rather than only those sections relating to Mr. Finkelman's recommendations. Over the course of the committee hearings the mood of the bargaining agents, realizing the scope and implications of their demands, changed. The Public Service Alliance of Canada at its appearance before the special joint committee requested the establishment by the government of a committee to study the Public Service Employment Act and make recommendations within two years.
In May of 1975 the Public Service Commission appeared again before the committee and supported the altered Alliance view. The Public Service Commission had modified its approach and, in its second submission to the special joint committee, recommended that a review of the Public Service Employment Act and the role of the commission be undertaken by a special task force, and immediate amendments to the Public Service Employment Act should be limited in the meantime to necessary technical adjustments. The committee concluded that the comprehensive re-evaluation of personnel management in the public service of Canada implicit in a review of the Public Service Employment Act was beyond its scope and resources.
Because of these representations and of the consensus reached as to the need for a comprehensive study of the issues and the alternatives which must be thoroughly assessed before parliament can deal with the Public Service Employment Act, the special joint committee recommended as follows:
1.	That a special task force be established to review the Public Service Employment Act and the role of the Commission in personnel management and employer-employee relations in the public service; and
2.	That the review include an examination of the role assigned the Public Service Commission and its relationship to the Treasury Board Secretariat and the Public Service Staff Relations Board.
3.	That the review entail a study of the relationship of the Public Service Commission and the departments and agencies; and consider the development of an audit system for performance accountability with respect to matters delegated to departments and agencies under the Public Service Employment Act.
The hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis) drew considerable attention, when he spoke in this House on Thursday of last week, to management in the public service. He made direct reference to the Public Service Commission when he said, as reported at page 1849 of Hansard:
December 13, 1976

The situation calls for a review of hiring practices ...
The situation calls for a meeting with the Public Service Commission to learn what measures the chairman of the Public Service Commission would like to see enacted in order that he can do his job. I believe that... the chairman of the Public Service Commission is saying... that he is hamstrung when he cannot know where vacancies are, when delegated authority has gone too far, when he has breaches of regulations on a scale admitted by the annual report of the Public Service Commission.
The hon. member for Ottawa West called upon the government to review the operation and to implement corrective measures. Four weeks ago the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) announced a drive to improve performance in the public service. When the use of a performance measurement system for the public service was first introduced by a former president of the treasury board a couple of years ago, I expressed my concern that it was being internally conceived and constructed. I expressed my doubts then, and I reiterate them today, that no matter how high the standard of efficiency developed within the public service, a question will remain in the minds of the general public if it seems that the very persons that are being measured are also those responsible for the system of measurement.
I should say here that there is obviously considerable concern in the public service itself that the criticisms which are being openly expressed today about hiring practices within the public service are reflecting upon the whole of the public service. Where there is abuse-and we have talked so much of abuse in other areas-there is always a reflection on the rest of the persons involved. This is unfair, and it is why these practices should be brought out into the open. This could easily be done if a committee were formed to study the question.
It is now almost four years since the start of the examination of the Public Service Staff Relations Act by Mr. Jacob Finkelman. We still have to see the introduction of legislation based on the recommendations which followed the study. It will be 1977, at best, before a task force is formed, if such a task force is to be formed, to examine the Public Service Employment Act. It was felt that the work of such a task force would take up to two years to complete. If previous procedure is followed, the report would go a committee which might deliberate for another year. Then the House would await the introduction of amending legislation. Thus, it could be 1980 before worth-while action is taken.
Since the tabling of the report of the special joint committee in February of this year, there has been little opportunity to debate in this House the many recommendations of the committee. I am aware that many members of the opposition would like to express their opinion of this subject, and I believe some of our own members who were on the Finkelman committee also desire to speak. This motion, which is based on the first three recommendations, has been introduced for the purpose of discussion, and I hope it will receive the support of members of all parties.

Mr. Speaker, it is customary to commend hon. members when they introduce good motions. This is generally done when the members are on our side of the House. It is more than courtesy and more than customary in respect of this motion to commend it most highly, having been brought to our attention by a member on the government side of the House.
I am delighted, through this motion, to have an opportunity to speak to this particular matter. Like the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert), I was a member of the Joint House and Senate Committee on Employer-Employee Relations in the Public Service when we examined together, more often in harmony than in disharmony, the problems we were confronted with on that occasion. The initiative the hon. member took on October 20 in formulating this particular motion was most timely, and our discussion today is even more timely in light of the discussions that have taken place in this House over the last three or four days, particularly on Thursday and Friday of last week.
Like the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis), who was likewise on that committee and has a deep interest in the public service, an interest which I share for reasons we have in common, both of us having been in the public service, I have a deep and abiding interest that the public service should continue to be a highly professional service providing to the Canadian people, in the best form possible, the service they require. When I joined what is now called the public service, it was known as the civil service. I felt at that time its role was to be civil and to serve. Now that it has gone public, I think it still should be civil and it still should serve. They are confronted, nonetheless, with tremendous difficulties. They have been facing great odds in the last four, five or six years, and the comments made in the debate on Thursday of last week by the hon. member for Ottawa West highlight and bring to our attention some of the odds faced by the public service today.
The morale in the public service, to my way of thinking, has dropped drastically and tragically, and a demoralized public service cannot offer the service it was once able to provide and be civil at the same time. This is most unfortunate. Perhaps I would not be out of place in saying that to a considerable extent the hon. member for Ottawa West shares my view that a lot of the blame can be related to the manner of implementing the recommendations of the Glassco report. Having served in the public service during those days, to my way of thinking there were too many changes imposed on the public service at the same time. Any large body of people can absorb one or two, preferably only one but at most two, changes at any one time, but to have thrust upon it a series of dramatic changes causes needless uncertainty about the future of careers. I submit this lies at the bottom of the demoralization within the public service and makes even more necessary the implementation of the suggestion of the hon. member for Vaudreuil of a task force to look into the Public Service Employment Act.
There were numerous changes imposed during the 1960s, and I suppose they are still going on. First of all, there was the

December 13, 1976
Public Service Employment Act management by objective notion, a complete change in the manner of preparing departmental budgets. On top of that, there were career futures involved in accepting, applying and learning a second language. This also required, in many instances, the departure from a position of a civil servant, some of them senior, from Ottawa to be immersed in the other language for about a year. The lack of contact with the department was in itself unsettling, and the relative ability to learn a second language, along with the difficulties and frustrations encountered as mature men and women in their 40s and 50s was distressing. This discovery on the part of mature men and women that, while they were capable administratively, they might not be capable at that age of picking up with ease a second language, caused needless distress.
Then there were the time studies undertaken in the departments at that time, and interdepartmental mobility, the ability of managers to shift members from one department to another or to claim members from other departments. These four serious and profound changes, being imposed upon the public service at one time, were the cause of a great deal of demoralization which, unfortunately, is noticeable.
The reorganization and the examination of the departments by management consultants, which in many instances resulted in the implantation of some of those who made the examination into the departments, had a tremendous effect. Management consultants found that there was a role for them in the departments and they made recommendations to that end. I have heard it said that there is one tower in the Lester B. Pearson Building for administration and another where the external policy is done.
This was not the situation as I knew it in External Affairs, where those of us who were foreign service officers still had administration work to do. On occasion we had administration to do abroad and when we were at home. Now a division has been made and people have been brought in laterally, at senior levels, and this, too, has caused considerable dissatisfaction and demoralization. There have been other incidents that one could quote. In CIDA, for example, the degree of demoralization was actually tabulated by a report requested by CIDA because of a rapid change of personnel. This report was never made public. An attempt was made to have it made public, but it was impossible to overcome the resistance in that particular instance. It is quite obvious that CIDA does not stand alone in the demoralization. There are in CIDA a number of dedicated officers. I could say that the majority of officers in CIDA are dedicated to the work they are doing, but the conditions under which they are obliged to work cause demoralization and frustration to the extent that many are retiring and seeking employment elsewhere. It is obvious, therefore, that we do need to have an examination of employment practices, whether they be departmental employment practices or the relationship between the Public Service Commission and the departments to ensure that this part of the demoralization at least can be eradicated.

It is my understanding that the public service commission's jurisdiction extends to deciding upon procedures for employment, hiring and firing, and promotions within the service whereas it is between Treasury Board and the management of departments and agencies to determine classification and selection. These three units of government have an interacting role which has not been clearly defined. They are the Public Service Commission on the one hand, Treasury Board and individual departments on the other, added to which must be, of course, the Public Service Staff Relations Board. There is needless conflict between the four agencies of government, and the reconciliation of their respective needs and their respective roles must take place. I suggest that it could well be done by the special task force requested by the hon. member for Vaudreuil.
Appeals are normally heard before the Public Service Commission, with representation on the board of appeal by the departmental officers concerned. I have had many complaints about the manner in which appeals on promotion have been rejected out of hand without taking account of, in any way, the representations made by the individual concerned. There could well be complaint, and it will not be easy to find-as the hon. member for Ottawa West would be the first to admit-the source and reality of the complaint. If nepotism or patronage exist, it will not be documented, and when those who might have been responsible, or who are thought to be responsible, are charged with it, they are bound to back away and completely disown responsibility. Yet if those problems exist, they must be examined.
I was heartened to hear that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) takes these charges very seriously. On the other hand, I was distressed to hear that he will do no more than find some way to inform the House. He refused to say that he would report to the House on these findings. I think this is a matter which not only parliament, but the Canadian public, should know about. If these practices exist, they should be made public; they should be open to those who pay for those services and who are not getting them in the manner that they require.
It is evident to me, therefore, that there is a great need to establish the interrelationship between the Public Service Commission, the Treasury Board and the Public Service Staff Relations Board so as to redefine the roles of each and the interrelationship that one has with the other. I recall mentioning to the former president of the treasury board, on one occasion when we were rushing to a committee, that his department, the treasury board, was a monster. He resented it. I maintain that it still deserves that appellation. It is a hydra-headed monster. It has been charged with too many roles, and if the task force can be established, it is the task force which could perhaps sever one or two of the hydra heads and produce a more meaningful Treasury Board and a more meaningful role for each of the agencies concerned with the employment, promotion and firing of public servants.
December 13, 1976

One other argument in favour of the task force is that it would offer the opportunity to many more members of the House to familiarize themselves with problems related to the public service. We must not forget that we are the largest employer in Canada. It is a large public service, and as a large public service it has many and large problems with which too few of us in the House are familiar.
Those of us who sat on the joint committee studying the Finkelman report found how many problems there were on the Public Service Staff Relations Board. I would venture to say that there are just as many in the Public Service Commission with which we should become familiar. I urge upon the House, therefore, to approve the motion that has been put forward by the hon. member for Vaudreuil, and I thank the House for giving me this opportunity to make these points.

Mr. Speaker, I have one or two points of emphasis that have not yet been made and which I should like to lay before the House, but before I do so I want to join the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) in commending the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) for bringing this motion before us this afternoon. Indeed, in spite of the tradition around here that private members' motions are talked out, I express the hope that this one might be allowed to pass.
After all, all that we would be doing by passing this motion this afternoon would be to express the opinion of the House that action should be taken along the lines already recommended by the Special Joint Committee of the Senate and the House of Commons on Employer-Employee relations in the Public Service which met for about a year and a half and placed its very considered proposals before the House. The report as a whole was not passed unanimously. When it came to a vote in the committee, I denied unanimity by disagreeing with some of the harsh recommendations with respect to the Public Service Staff Relations Act. However, we were unanimous with respect to the points which are before us this afternoon, namely, a call for a task force and a general review of the Public Service Employment Act and of the activities of the Public Service Commission and its relation to various other bodies. So I hope we can say this afternoon that we want this action to be taken.
I thought the hon. member for Vaudreuil used particularly good judgment in making a short speech, but in that short speech he said what needed to be said, namely, that time has been flitting by while the problems remain.
Our committee sat for about a year and a half. It took a year and a half or two years to get the committee started. Now we are well into the second session, and there is no sign yet either of the bills which were recommended in that report or of this task force, so I hope some action will be taken very soon. That has been said by the two previous speakers. I endorse it, so I need not spell it out; I need not add anything further to that part of the argument.

I know that persons like the hon. member opposite and the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis) do not wish to tar the whole group of public servants, but this kind of thing develops, and I simply want to take a moment or two to say again that, as far as I am concerned, the public servants who work for the government and the people of Canada are workers just like workers in the CPR and CNR shops in my riding, or workers in any shop, plant or industry across the country.
Public servants are doing their best under the directions they are given and under the conditions which are created for them, and they deserve our defence. They deserve not to be the subject of an attack in this place or in the press. They are a good lot and, as I say, we could not do our work as members of parliament if we did not have public servants to back us up in the things we are called upon to do.
The other thing I want to say is that I get the feeling that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was almost happy the other day to pick up the issue which had been raised, and other ministers have done the same, because the suggestion is that perhaps the troubles the government has are not of the government's own making. In the final analysis the persons at the top have responsibility, and the blame for the poor conditions, the lack of morale, the feeling that the government and other things are falling apart, rests not with the middle or lower public servants, and not even with some who are up the ladder a bit, but with the government itself. The final responsibility rests with the cabinet ministers opposite, and I have no use for any attempt on the part of the government to avoid that responsibility by finding a scapegoat in the public service.
I support the motion. I hope the House will pass it this afternoon, but I wanted to say those two things. I defend the public servants of this country, and I refuse to let the government get off the hook for the trouble in which it finds itself.

Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief because I too would like to see the House approve this motion. However, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has already pointed out, it is only a recommendation put forward for government consideration.
I am one of those who served on the joint committee. The result of a lot of very useful work is sitting, waiting to be dealt
1954

December 13, 1976
Public Service Employment Act
with, and I often wonder who "they" are, for whom all this work is waiting. The point is that nothing seems to have happened, and time is going by. There was a degree of urgency, and it is quite correct that there was unanimity with respect to the recommendations which led to the basis for the hon. member's presentation to us.
I would like to point out to hon. members that this motion should be approved, and I hope hon. members who speak will speak briefly. It should be approved, if for no other reason than to indicate to the government that there is growing concern in the public service.
There is a growing recognition of the need for amendments not only to the Public Service Staff Relations Act but also for a review of the Public Service Commission. As did the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, I have two reasons for wanting to see this motion passed. While I share the concern of the previous speaker that we should not tar people in the public service of Canada with thoughtless acts or words, nevertheless problems do arise. One of those which concerns me is the growing proliferation of personnel service contracts in the public service of Canada. I recall the chairman of the Public Service Commission, Mr. Carson, indicating to us that he did not know how many there were, he did not know what they were doing, he did not know what they were being paid, and he was uncertain of their relationship to the personnel administration system. In short, there was very little evidence he could give us except to indicate clearly to us that he was afraid he did not have control over them, and that a continuation of this as a widespread practice could lead to an impairment of the usefulness of the Public Service Commission. That is my first reason.
My second reason can be expressed more briefly. We were pressured to complete our work. There was a great sense of urgency about completing the study of employer-employee relations in the public service. Some of us wanted to stretch it out a bit longer to make sure it was fully understood, fully tested, probed and scrutinized by those people involved, but no, we had to finish our work, and in late May we completed our report. Now it sits there. If there was such urgency to complete the report, why has there been such foot dragging and delay in the establishment of the task force? The joint committee felt it was of sufficient importance and urgency that it formed the first three or four recommendations of that committee to this House. I pose this as a question.
Having said that, I will sit down, and I hope that government backbenchers will not talk this matter out. There is a sense of urgency. I think it is clear to most of us, certainly to people outside Ottawa, that there is a growing withdrawal of 100 per cent total moral support for the administration of Canada if it is to be by senior public servants. I think it is incumbent upon us to recognize our responsibility and to take initiatives and steps which can correct and reverse this.
With that I again commend the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) and indicate to him that I am very pleased to stand here and lend him what support I can on this particular matter.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to make a lengthy speech today in this House. I would, however, like to make two or three points in the debate.
I was pleased with the remarks of the two previous speakers, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall), who indicated that they are concerned, as we all are, about the possible effects of poor morale in the Public Service of Canada.
I hope that nothing I have said in this place or elsewhere will be construed as a reflection upon the public service itself. I believe the Canadian public service has one of the highest standards in the world. Having said that, however, I think it is in the interests of the public service and the public-in fact it is our duty according to our conscience-to expose those situations which have come to our attention.
I have endeavoured to call attention to the lack of review of hiring practices and the very serious consequences of this. It was with no little concern that I read in the press over the week end some examples of horror stories. Of course in every large organization which employs hundreds of thousands of people there will be some irregularities, but to suggest that all senior civil servants are corrupt or that there is a widespread practice of female employees gaining advancement by sex and favouritism is wrong. I have used the expression "bureaucratic patronage"; I want to make it abundantly clear that we are talking about a small minority situation. If these situations exist at all, however, it is of the most serious importance to the people of Canada.
The second point I should like to make is that there is unanimity of this matter. Every member who has spoken, and all of us who have served on the committee-I served for over a year on the joint committee of the House and the other place reviewing employer-employee relations in the public service- all of us without exception were impressed by the pleas made by the Chairman of the Public Service Commission who appeared personally before the committee. He said in the strongest possible terms that there should be consequential amendments to the Public Service Employment Act as a result of what has to be done with the Public Service Staff Relations Act. He said that he hoped the government would take the opportunity to set up a task force with broad terms of reference to review the entire operation of the Public Service Employment Act. I know that the individual concerned, and his successor in this post, are greatly concerned that such a task force or something equivalent to it should be appointed. I urge the government in the strongest terms to pay heed to these recommendations. I am confident that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is taking them seriously and I look forward to an announcement before very long in this place or somewhere else of the steps that will be taken. I hope they will be along the lines of the recommendations put before us today.
I cannot leave the subject without taking the opportunity to say a word or two about the operation of Data Stream in the
December 13, 1976

public service. The attempt to computerize hiring, promotion, and other operations within the Public Service of Canada, in my opinion has had some very unfortunate side effects. As a member of this House I am in no position to pass final judgment on the operation of data streaming, but I have heard so many complaints about the rewards going to those who learn the Data Stream language. Senior civil servants have told me that the best thing young persons entering the public service can do is spend a week learning all about the coded data that goes into the Data Strean and make sure their files are coded according to the most recent jargon. Then their files will be pulled out when all the bright opportunities turn up. If that is the case then the matter has to be examined.
If it is the case that the recruiting officers who go to the universities really do not know where the vacancies are, and their operation consists of interviewing bright young men and women coming out of our universities each year, drawing up their case histories and feeding them into the data stream, then there is something greatly wrong with the process. I do not believe that recruiting officers with this kind of inadequate information can give proper advice and serve the recruiting function which is their responsibility in the proper way if their information is limited.
I would hope that the task force, or whatever is established-perhaps a special committee-would look at the side effects, the undesirable effects that are the object of so many complaints about the computerizing of the hiring process and the promotion process.
I commend the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert). I think he has done a service by picking out this particular aspect of the committee's report and bringing about a debate in this place. There are those who say that the private members' hour is a useless exercise. I know the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre will smile at this because he has heard me rise in this place on many occasions and say I did not think it served very much of a useful purpose. I do not think he has heard me do that in this parliament, however.

speechtext: Well, I do not believe so at all. I think the hon. member opposite put his finger on the important point when he said that the people in the government are responsible in this area. The government has been given the mandate to show responsibility and government members should ask deputy ministers questions, the answers to which might reveal certain difficulties in the civil service. speechtext:
Questions should be asked about hirings. Deputy ministers should be asked, "Have there been any grievances in this department? Have any raised objections to advertisements for new positions?" The answers to such questions would quickly test morale. Such questions should be asked now, at this instant, instead of having some outside committee look at each department.
It is important for the government to discover if deputy ministers and those in management firmly understand what is happening among those in lower management positions, and even among ordinary working people. Mr. Speaker, the sort of

thing complained of in the government also happens in ordinary business. One hears that even in such well known companies as Bell Telephone serious difficulties have occurred. At one time an operator used to be able to call up a telephone subscriber and say, "Your telephone bill is overdue." Now the operator must get permission from the supervisor to make that call; the supervisor in turn must get permission from the supervisor of unpaid bills, and the manager must O.K. that call. Only then may the call be made by the operator. Even so, sometimes some other manager will not allow that call to be made and the subscriber is allowed to retain his telephone. Therefore the person in the front line of the business, so to speak, does not have the opportunity to serve properly.
I venture to suggest that people working behind desks in the Unemployment Insurance Commission and other branches of the civil service are not allowed to make decisions. Sometimes hon. members opposite go to bat with the minister on behalf of some person who has been dealt with unjustly. In that case the member of parliament will get the credit for helping some poor soul. Yet if it were not for some foolish regulation, the person behind the desk could have dealt with the matter and might have been given credit for being a true civil servant. And this should be happening. We should allow our civil servants once again to be servants of the public and not the servants of the management above them. This is the great problem we face. It can best be solved by the people responsible, the people I will hold responsible and who will ultimately have to pay for any indiscretions which occur in that area.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have achieved many things in my speeches, but I have never before stopped the clock. I suppose that can be interpreted that I can go on forever and the clock will remain as it is.
Perhaps I might be permitted to recap before I get into the conclusion of my remarks. I had suggested that this bill is no more than a show of the usual flim-flam for which the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Faulkner) is well known. I said that I do not believe the bill as it stands or in its proposals will do anything of any great significance in terms of improving the ability of our scientists to do research in this country. It will not increase the funding which is required as a very fundamental step if science and technology in Canada are to progress at the rate we are hoping to see.
The government's policy has not changed from one science minister to the next and the latest edition does not seem to be pursuing matters very much differently. With this particular government, the situation has been created in Canada whereby the scientist is becoming a vanishing species. Perhaps the minister should be placing the research scientists of Canada on the endangered list, along with a number of other creatures that have been disappearing very quickly from the Canadian scene. An example of this is medical research. Some years ago the tradition was that about 5 per cent, or one out of every 20 medical graduates, went into the research field. Today the number is almost zero. Virtually none of them are choosing research as a career because of the severe instability and insecurity that surround the research community as a result of no policies being introduced by this government.
To get back to the specifics, before the evening break I was making some comment on the structures being proposed, and making some other suggestions. The news releases of the Ministry of Science and Technology refer to the establishment of an inter-council co-ordinating committee. I discussed this a little, but want to make a few more comments about it. It appears that this particular structure will have no status
Scientific Activities of Government whatsoever in the legislation and will therefore be unable to exert any authority over the activities of the responsible "designated ministers". Without exercising budgetary control, the proposed inter-council co-ordinating committee can hardly be expected to perform any useful function effectively.
The proposed terms of reference for the two new research councils are highly imprecise with regard both to their objectives and the functions which they are expected to perform. At least these should be elaborated on to the same extent as for the Science Council or the Canada Council. More particularly there appears to be nothing to prevent them from establishing research laboratories in their own right, which would be highly redundant. Accordingly it seems desirable to explicitly limit their activities to the provision of grants and scholarships.
Something that everyone involved in research feels we need is a science policy. We need a science policy from the short term as well as the long term point of view. From the short term point of view it appears the government has opted to cut research spending, using the excuse that this is somehow in harmony with the restraint program. But while cutting expenditures on research might be politically advantageous in the short run, it will produce tremendous disadvantages in the long run since the country will be losing a great opportunity to benefit from advances in industrial technology. Either we invest in scientific research now and reap substantial benefits later, or we cut spending on research and become a deteriorating society with little hope of achieving such substantial gains in the industrial area.
The minister might be of the opinion that research funds could be better spent on humanitarian projects such as those favoured by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) who wants everyone to have a guaranteed annual income. But it seems to me this would be a backward step because in order to sustain a humanitarian society in modern times there must be a sound economy based on modern technology. We are obviously lagging behind the efforts of other countries in the western world in this field.
When the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) went to Japan not long ago, and to Europe somewhat earlier, he implied that we in Canada have a great deal of scientific technology to market. Yet we are winding down expenditure on research while doing business with the Japanese who have a great deal of expertise behind them. To represent Canada as making a similar effort suggests a lack of sincerity on the part of the right hon. gentleman. In any case, his statements in Japan, as far as they concern our scientific commitment, are not in keeping with the actions he is taking back home.
There are one or two matters I wish to deal with specifically. One of them has to do with tariff charges affecting goods which are used in research-chemicals and so on. Tariff item 69605-1 relates to such material, also used in teaching at the universities and elsewhere. Formerly these products were exempt from tariff, but the federal government apparently decided it did not wish to subsidize this aspect of teaching and

December 13, 1976
Scientific Activities of Government withdrew the concession. The direct result has been an increase of 10 per cent in the cost of chemistry research and a 5 or 6 per cent increase in the cost of medical research. This is surely an example of the government taking a step without thinking it through. A directive has been issued to customs officers by a senior bureaucrat to the effect that if the user (or the researcher) personally orders chemicals he may be able to get around this charge. But in order to do so he would be obliged to indicate specifically how the material was to be used and describe the research project in some detail. A procedure of that kind is totally unworkable, Mr. Speaker.
The minister has given the impression that he is thinking of revising the estimate for 1977-78. It would appear he has not let anybody know about this except those of us who sit in the House. He is either unaware of the way in which the council operates or he is being dishonest. I say this because although the grants are made in April they reflect decisions which are being made today or which will be made shortly. I suggest that if there is to be an increase he should inform the councils concerned, letting them know what the increase is to be, 6 per cent, 8 per cent or 20 per cent-so that proper planning can be undertaken.
I would also remind the minister-if he is listening-that should he be planning to increase grants in keeping with the rise in the consumer price index, the consumer price index has been increasing at a much slower rate in the past few months than has the index reflecting the cost of research and research materials. I am told that inflation in this area averages out to 15 per cent. Thus, simply to keep purchasing power at last year's level he would need to announce an increase of 15 per cent as a minimum. But the hon. gentleman has not done this. He has restricted himself to a generalization which may raise people's hopes, but so far he has not said anything worth while.
I wish to make one more point in the area of scientific research. It concerns the equipment used. I am told by representatives of the various research organizations that as far as equipment is concerned we are living on borrowed time. The average lifetime of research equipment is a decade or so, and most of our machinery is six or seven years old. We are getting ourselves into a situation where everything will need to be replaced at the same time, just as is happening in the field of national defence. If the minister does not want to be faced with a call for exceptionally heavy capital outlay for equipment all at once he should make it possible for a certain amount of our equipment to be renewed every year.
With regard to the Medical Research Council, the suggestion is that its terms of reference be broadened to include public health research while otherwise remaining essentially the same. I am not objecting to that. The public health function has been carried out by the Department of National Health and Welfare itself in the past, but it is not clear from the bill whether the responsibility will be taken over by the Medical Research Council. If so, will there be a similar transfer of funds to the Medical Research Council? In other words, can the minister assure the House, or can he assure me if not everybody else, that responsibility for research into

public health will not simply put additional pressure and strain on funds for research, which are already in short supply, in the budget of the Medical Research Council? If there is going to be this added responsibility, we must have a commitment from the minister that additional funds will be made available. Of course the minister did not make any mention of that in his comments.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare is presently responsible for the Medical Research Council, but who is the minister responsible for each of the other research councils? I have already touched once on this matter. I should like to know why there is reluctance to tell us. Rather than say it will be under some designated minister, why not tell the House who will be responsible?
I see my time has more or less expired, Mr. Speaker, so I will conclude-

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I first of all congratulate the government on the speed with which it has brought forward this legislation. It arose out of the recommendations of the special Senate committee on science policy eight or nine years ago, and was followed very quickly by a promise in the throne speech of 1974 by the present Minister of Communications (Mrs. Sauve), the twice removed Minister of State for Science and Technology. There was going to be an important reorganization which would enable this ministry to look after science and technology in this country which would ensure us all a great and glorious future. Considering the fanfare that introduced this ministry in 1971, and considering the statements made from time to time by the four, now five, ministers who have filled this portfolio since its inception-

that the government considers science and technology an extremely low priority; that the government has no understanding of the necessity for a science policy for this country and for Canada having technological competence.
It is very difficult to look at this piece of primary evidence or production from the Department of State for Science and Technology, Bill C-26, as giving us any idea about what is the government's overall direction in science and technology matters. Perhaps that is in keeping with what the immediate past minister of science and technology said last June, namely, that MOSST:
-is a low profile organization whose influence will not be detected in individual issues so much as in the general trend of government policy and action in science.
That is another way of saying that government has no comprehensive science policy. In fact MOSST has been so low profile that the ministry has basically conceded defeat in detailing a comprehensive science policy, confining its actions to restructuring already existing institutions.
In Bill C-26 we see provisions that cannot serve as any reasonable facsimile of a science policy. It is-

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION (SCIENTIFIC ACTIVITIES) ACT, 1976 MEASURE RESPECTING ORGANIZATION OF CERTAIN SCIENTIFIC ACTIVITIES OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Yes, science fiction, as my colleague from Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) says, I think very appropriately. This simply is not enough. We in Canada have not only an opportunity but a tremendous need at this time to create an economic future for the country, and in order to achieve that goal a good technological base is absolutely essential. That is not one man's opinion; that is the opinion of such learned groups as the Science Council of Canada, the Economic Council of Canada, the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development, and indeed the opinion of every individual or group of individuals or organization that has looked at science and technology in Canada over the recent past. There have been literally scores of investigations, and without exception each has led to a criticism of Canada's performance in this area and to recommendations for more emphasis to be placed by the government on science and technology. This has been met with silence by the government. There has been no initiative or movement whatsoever.
It is obvious that the government simply has no understanding or appreciation of science and technology. If it were not so important in terms of its long-term consequences to the country, it would almost be laughable, Mr. Speaker. The previous minister described it as a low profile organization, which is another way of saying a non-productive, do nothing organization. I think the description of the Minister of State for Science and Technology is a pretty accurate one. If in fact science and technology are to continue to be given the same level of priority by the government, the Canadian public would be far better off disbanding the department. It is supposedly responsible for science and technology, but this is a facade, a deception.
The Canadian people are being deceived into believing that the government has a minister and a ministry examining and
Scientific Activities of Government recommending policies, helping to implement programs to ensure that we remain in the twentieth century at the forefront of technology, which is so necessary in this highly competitive world. But that has not been the case, and this sort of deception of the Canadian public is most inappropriate in our system.
When I say deception, what do I mean? Let me examine the history of this department. It was established in 1971, and finally in the summer of 1972, after some period of gestation, it brought forward a new policy called the policy of contracting out to industry. In one of the background papers produced by the then minister, who is now Mnister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie), the government stated as follows:
The policy of intensified contracting-out of R & D to the private sector was developed when the federal government came to the conclusion that more R & D in industry offered a means of creating new technologies which, in turn, would help stimulate the economy and provide jobs.
Other factors in the government's decision:
(1)	That industry in Canada invested a much smaller share of the gross national product in research and development than most industrialized nations, less than half the proportion invested in Britain, in the United States and Japan.
(2)	That the federal government has contributed less proportionately to R & D performed in the business sector than some other industrialized countries but not all. For instance, Britain, France and Germany have underwritten a larger portion of the R & D performed in industry than has Canada. On the other hand, the Japanese government has contributed less.
(3)	Canada ranks far below Sweden, the U.S., Germany, Belgium, Britain, Japan, the Netherlands and France in percentage of R & D carried out by business on its own behalf.
(4)	Only 30 per cent of industrial R & D establishments employ more than five scientists or engineers. Thus 70 per cent employ five or fewer graduates. Only 17 of roughly 700 such establishments employ 50 professionals or more.
It goes on in the same vein up to nine points castigating Canada's performance in research and development in science and technology, and this is a background paper put out by the Department of the Minister of State for Science and Technology. This was all to be changed by the policy of contracting out.
That policy was introduced in August 1972, and between then and 1976 the percentage of in-house government spending on R and D actually increased. This contracting out program was designed to decrease the persentage of in-house research and development expenditure by this government, but in fact it increased. The government's performance was exactly contrary to the one statement of policy it had made.
The government and the minister were complaining about the fact that Canada spent so much less on research and development than other countries. What has happened since that time? At the time the policy was announced the government spent 1.22 per cent of its gross national product on research and development, one of the worst records in the western world. The government was aware of this and said so in this document. It brought out a new policy and a new ministry, and great things were to happen. In 1974 that percentage had dropped to 0.84 per cent. It had declined, as pointed out by my colleague, the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk), who immediately preceded me in this debate,
