Scientific Activities of Government in all areas of medical research, scientific research and so on, and our performance has deteriorated steadily since then. I do not have those figures to make that comparison, but it is obvious the performance has deteriorated. This problem the government expressed such concern about in 1972 has grown worse.
To add insult to injury, if you like, the second time the minister ventured forth on this subject was in the throne speech of 1974. It talks about how important this ministry is going to be and all the great new authority it is to have, and how science and technology will take off because of this important new role that the Minister of State for Science and Technology was going to play within the Government of Canada. That was in the throne speech of 1974. Anyone who examines the speech made by the then minister, now the Minister of Communications, and compares the promises with performance has to be a little bit disgusted.
Then the third big piece of action by this ministry was last August 5 in the form of a news release sent out by the immediate predecessor to the present minister. It states that C. M. Drury, Minister of State for Science and Technology, announced that the government had reaffirmed its policy to encourage industrial participation to the fullest extent in its scientific program. That was the great new declaration of intent of August 5, 1976.
If we examine the document produced by the department which demonstrates this contracting out program, and we look at the latest figures available up to August 31, 1976, we see that as of October 31, 1975, the government had contracted out for $67 million worth of research; and up to August 31, 1976, it had contracted out for $38.7 million. That is 58 per cent of what it had done last year, a reduction of 42 per cent. This comes after the press release of August 5 telling us about this great new program. If the government was not using our money and if there were not 23 million Canadians out there depending on this government to show some semblance of knowledge about what is taking place, this really would be laughable. Here we have this great Ministry of State for Science and Technology which is supposed to .look after our future in this area. By my count, and I have kept track of everything done since it started, this ministry has made three statements of intent in five years. I have not figured out how much this has cost us in total, but I would guess around $20 million in terms of salaries. The department has made three statements of intent and in every single case the promises and the performance have gone in exactly opposite directions. In baseball after three strikes you are out. The most generous and humane thing that could happen to this department would be to send it out as well because it is a terrible waste of the taxpayers' money and is a totally useless department.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION (SCIENTIFIC ACTIVITIES) ACT, 1976 MEASURE RESPECTING ORGANIZATION OF CERTAIN SCIENTIFIC ACTIVITIES OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Rubbish!

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION (SCIENTIFIC ACTIVITIES) ACT, 1976 MEASURE RESPECTING ORGANIZATION OF CERTAIN SCIENTIFIC ACTIVITIES OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
That is not to say the job the department is supposed to perform is in the same category. Quite the opposite is true.

My party has gone on record on many occasions calling for cuts and reductions in government spending in every area except science and technology. If members opposite had bothered to examine statements by my leader and by spokesmen for our party, they would have seen that we consider science and technology vitally important to Canada's future. We are committed to dramatically expanding expenditures in this important area. We encourage a dramatic increase in expenditures in this area within the private sector. It is obvious that the government feels just the opposite. A moment ago one hon. member opposite shouted out "rubbish" when I suggested that perhaps the kindest thing we could do is wind up this department. Let me quote back to the hon. member words from the speech on June 9 of this year as follows:
First, on a per capita basis Canada is among the world's leading net exporters of raw materials and among the leading net importers of manufactured products.
Then it went on to describe the situation in Canada, and said:
.. . among OECD countries only Ireland has a smaller proportion than Canada of its work force employed in the secondary sector.
.. . among ten countries compared by the OECD for their performance in technological innovation, Canada ranked in the tenth and last position.
.. . Canada has a huge trade deficit in the category of management and technological services. Our deficit of trade in business services in engineering oriented industries is over $1 billion per year .. .
In addition, recent trends in industrial research and development expenditures indicate that our industrial technological capability may be declining. Since 1969 research and development expenditures in Canadian industry have remained essentially constant at about $400 million per year, resulting in a substantial decline in the research and development to sales ratio.
These are the remarks not of a member of an opposition party, but of a member of the Liberal party describing how the government he supports has developed science and technology in this country. I challenge any hon. member opposite to examine Canada's performance in this area, and I challenge any hon. member opposite who can read to read the proceedings of the Senate Science Committee, the members of which are supporters of the government party, to read these debates and to read what their own Senators have been saying about the science policy of the government they support. I challenge them to do so and then, in all honesty, to stand up here and say that this government deserves a pat on the back for the great things it is doing for science and technology. Perhaps, on the other hand, I should not offer this challenge because it is pretty easy for a Liberal to take it up in spite of what the true facts really are, just as they do every day in all sorts of areas.
This bill hardly warrants the time of the House. It is like moving furniture, shifting chairs or putting a new coat of paint on an old wall. It accomplishes nothing, and since we already have a ministry of state perpetrating a fraud on the Canadian people by claiming to act responsibly in terms of science and technology in this country, to perpetrate another fraud by claiming this bill will do great things is not something that should make us as legislators proud because it is a nothing bill.
This is tragic because there are so many areas in terms of the quality of life, the value and importance of science, and so on, which should be commented upon and have been comment-
December 13, 1976

ed upon by some of my colleagues. The simple fact is that last year our trade deficit in high technology goods amounted to $8.5 billion, and the prediction for this year is that it will amount to $10 billion. This should cause a responsible government to take some action to reverse that. Science and technology are not the total answer, but they are at the foundation of any long-term solution, and the failure of the government to appreciate and understand that is tragic and is a source of great concern to any thinking Canadian.
I should like to say in conclusion that it must be recognized by the government that science and technology, and therefore the science policy, are far too important to Canada's future to allow for a continuation of the ad hoc approaches of the government. If history can teach us anything, it is that in the twentieth century a country's technological competence more than any other factor determines that nation's role and position in the world. A subject of this import deserves more attention from and concern of those establishing public policy than is shown in this legislation or than has been shown by this government since the Ministry of State for Science and Technology has been established.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION (SCIENTIFIC ACTIVITIES) ACT, 1976 MEASURE RESPECTING ORGANIZATION OF CERTAIN SCIENTIFIC ACTIVITIES OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I say at the outset that I welcome the opportunity to make a few brief comments on Bill C-26, an act respecting the organization of certain scientific activities of the Government of Canada. Initially I would like to make a few observations regarding the reorganization of the scientific activities as they are outlined in the bill before us. Secondly, I would like to comment on what I would interpret as three unanswered questions which, in my view, are germane to this debate and to the legislation before us.
The first question is: what is the future of the Ministry of State for Science and Technology? That is particularly germane, not only in terms of what has happened in the past but, as I noticed, the bill was introduced today in the name of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and, if my memory serves me correctly, the bill is to be referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates. Frankly, I believe there is a message even in the small comment made by the minister at the outset of his remarks.
The second question that is germane to this debate is: what is the government's immediate and long-term financial commitment to medical research and development?
The third question that must be asked and explored is: what is the government's science and research policy in Canada? I think it is obvious to anyone who has looked at this area that without specific answers to these three questions that I have raised the legislation before us is meaningless. It offers no reassurance to the scientific community that stability will exist in the future. It offers no reassurance that the government is aware of the importance of research and development in Canada and that it has established research and development as a priority item.
The major recommendation in the bill is the creation of a new granting council, the so-called social sciences and humani-
Scientific Activities of Government ties research council. The establishment of this council is in keeping with the changes that were suggested in the throne speech of 1974, with one major exception. In the bill before us the minister has not been named. I want to emphasize again that the minister for that most important council has not been named. In 1974 it was the intention of the government to separate social sciences and humanities from the Canada Council which is responsible to the Secretary of State, and to place them under the jurisdiction of the Minister of State for Science and Technology.
Notwithstanding the arguments for or against separating the social sciences and humanities from the arts, I suggest that it is extremely critical to know the minister responsible for the granting policies of that particular council. If, for example, the granting policy regarding humanities and social sciences is placed under the Minister of State for Science and Technology and removed from the responsibility of the Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts), where it was associated with a context of cultural policy, that would be a very major shift which I suggest may prove to be disadvantageous. Frankly, I do not see the logic of leaving the designation of the minister in limbo, or what may prove to be more disastrous in the future, the prospect of shifting the ministry from time to time at the whim of the government. I suggest to the minister in all sincerity the importance, for two reasons, of naming the minister responsible for this new granting council, the social sciences and humanities council. First, it would ensure greater stability in the future with respect to that granting council and, more important, it would provide not only to members of parliament but also to Canadians the opportunity to assess objectively the future granting policies of this particular council which is anticipated.
A second recommendation in the bill is the formation of a natural sciences and engineering research council, and I want to say to the minister that in my view this is a distinct improvement over the announcement in the throne speech of 1974 in which there was to be the formation of a natural science research council. It was apparent at the time of that announcement that the entire field of engineering research and development had been almost ignored and relegated to an insignificant role. Of course this view was reinforced by a letter I received from a Mr. C. A. Campbell, president of the Association of Professional Engineers of the Province of Ontario, in May of 1974. The same letter was probably received by other hon. members of this House and probably by the minister. In that letter the concerns of the membership, which totals approximately 35,000 engineers who are active in a variety of fields in various areas of the province, were expressed. However, I want to draw to the attention of the minister that in that letter from Mr. Campbell it is stated:
It is recommended that the importance of engineering be appropriately recognized by renaming the first of the proposed granting councils as "The Natural Science and Engineering Research Council" and by ensuring that the terms of reference of that council require it to give as strong emphasis to engineering research as it does to natural sciences research, with commensurate allocation of resources.

December 13, 1976
Scientific Activities of Government
As I indicated previously, the naming of the council is a distinct improvement over what was announced in the throne speech of 1974. However, the functions of the newly formed council as defined in the legislation, and certainly as I understand it, are to promote and assist research in the natural sciences other than the health services. There is no mention of engineering research and development. Obviously the name is meaningless with respect to the new council unless the terms of reference recognize the importance of engineering research, a component of the new council, and I hope that before the termination of this debate the minister will clarify this apparent discrepancy between the name of the council and the functions of the council as they relate to the field of engineering and as defined in the bill which is before us.
Perhaps when the minister responds to that particular point, he might also address himself to another proposal which was raised by the engineering association from Ontario. In that same letter to which I previously referred it is also stated:
The proposal to vest in the Royal Society of Canada full responsibility for the maintenance of relationships between Canadian and international engineering organizations is of particular concern to all engineers. It is suggested most forcibly that such activities, if they are to be appropriately productive, must be assigned to an organization properly representative of the engineering community in Canada. The Canadian Council of Professional Engineers, in whose constituent licensing bodies 75,000 engineers are registered, is such a body.
I think that is a most important proposal which is made by that particular professional body, and perhaps the minister will respond to that recommendation.
The minister responsible for this new granting agency has not been designated, and as I described previously with regard to the other granting council, I view this with some degree of skepticism because of the instability and uncertainty which I believe may be fostered in the granting policies of that council without some stability from a designated minister.
A third feature of the bill before us is the proposed changes to the Medical Research Council Act. As I understand the proposed amendments, the present restrictions preventing the Medical Research Council from supporting research in the public health field will be removed. This will effectively permit the Medical Research Council to fund research activities in the area of health care delivery.
As I have indicated in the past on numerous occasions in the House in various debates and questions, research in the area of health care delivery should be an important component of medical research, provided that we sustain and build a strong research base. Indeed it is my firm belief that if we are to attain scientific excellence in the area of health care delivery research, a very significant number of such scientists will have demonstrated previous success in basic research activities. Again, however, there is a new amendment to the Medical Research Council Act which I view with some concern and a good deal of skepticism. It is the part which deals with the minister responsible for the act. The present bill indicates that the minister will be designated by the Governor in Council, which I suggest could possibly be a major change in terms of future policy.

If the Medical Research Council is to continue under the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde), that is an entirely different matter than relating to the government, say, through the portfolio of the Minister of State for Science and Technology. The latter would be a very significant change which would probably result in substantive changes in the function of the Medical Research Council over a period of time.
While I am dealing with the Medical Research Council, I should point out that on numerous occasions in the past we have shown in very clear terms the government's lack of interest in the Medical Research Council, and the government's lack of leadership in providing a medical research base across Canada which would ensure the quality of medical education and the quality of health care to which Canadians are entitled.
To much of the material which has been presented to this House in the past I want to add a new caveat. Recent events have indicated to me that the government is not interested in establishing national medical research standards, which I believe are very important. In response to the disregard of the federal government, if I may use that word, for the future of medical research, the province of Ontario has indicated that it is planning to provide through the provincial lottery approximately $50 million per year to be devoted to health research and health related research programs, including environmental health, occupational medicine, et cetera. It is obvious that Ontario has realized that scientific activities in Canada, and certainly in that province, are substandard, are deteriorating, and the province of Ontario is prepared to take the necessary action to reverse that particular trend.
I want to point out that it is readily apparent that with the infusion of a minimum of at least $50 million into the medical research area in Ontario, which I must emphasize is roughly equivalent to the Medical Research Council budget, there will be an interference with the federal presence in research and a potential for the balkanization of research activities in Canada.
Of major concern is the fact that the federal government has not viewed the matter in the national public interest and is prepared to abdicate its responsibility rather than promote federal-provincial discussions to ensure that research activity and over-all national standards will be maintained in this most important area.
The fourth feature of the bill is related to the Science Council of Canada. When the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Faulkner) issued a news release on December 2, he indicated that the science council is to have its mandate restated to provide it with a clear national and public information role. I want to repeat that, Mr. Speaker-to have its mandate restated to provide it with a clear national public information role. Frankly, I do not grasp the significance of that statement. I must say in all sincerity it has been my
December 13, 1976

personal view that the Science Council of Canada has been performing that function in the past.
Perhaps the minister envisages a new role for the science council in terms of public information. I could give two examples that I think the minister should examine. Perhaps this is what he is referring to and he will enlighten the House on this subject later in the debate. I would refer him to an article that appeared in the Montreal Gazette of September 30, 1976, under the heading "Public Information Act Urged by Science Head". I think it is pertinent and something we should look at in terms of public information and perhaps the role of the science council. The article reads as follows:
The executive director of the Science Council of Canada came out here yesterday in support of a freedom of information act.
"This increasingly public process is vital to the health of a system which otherwise might tend to become technocratic and centralist," John Shepherd told the Association of Consulting Engineers of Canada.
"From an industrial point of view, the overriding mandatory requirement is that we accept this 'fish-bowl' concept and that we plunge into the public debate with energy."
In the future, issues will be greatly influenced-if not decided-in the public forum, he added.
"Whatever the hesitancies, and whatever the actual level of skepticism, the process is extremely positive, and we should move to it rather than either withdraw or comply at minimum levels," Shepherd said, adding: "But it does pose problems."
The tone of the debate is frequently negative and reactive, he said, adding that this could perhaps be attributed to the fact that the public often does not receive adequate information about projects.
The desire to attract attention causes protesters to cast decision makers as villains, committed to a project which those opposed characterize as completely alien to the public interest.
In such a process, the motives of major participants in a project may be brought under question and scrutiny "by groups which are becoming more and more professional in the arts of public dialogue."
Enormous benefits would accrue if the government sent working papers on policy positions to affected groups for comment.
The sense of participation in the decision process "would in my view be revolutionary in its possible impact on government business relations," said Shepherd.
If the minister is visualizing information in that context then I think it is a positive step. I would remind the minister, however, that on May 13 this year, in an opposition day debate concerned with science, I addressed myself to the specific problem of the important challenges of our generation in terms of the immensity of the technological revolution and its relationship to people in our institutions. In all sincerity I would ask the minister to refer to page 13493 of Hansard for May 13, 1976, and read that part of the speech I gave at that time. I say that because I think it is an important element that the government has ignored in the past, and it may well serve as an important component in an important area for the science council in the future.
As I indicated at the outset, the present legislation may prove meaningless unless three specific questions are answered. The first question is related to the future role of the Ministry of Science and Technology. I must say that although significant changes are proposed in the legislation which has the potential for sweeping alterations in science in Canada, in my view there are too many unanswered questions which make it
Scientific Activities of Government
impossible at this time to determine the direction that science will take in Canada. Frankly, and I say this with all due respect to the minister, I am not convinced that the recent cabinet shuffle and the return to a full time minister of science and technology will give rise to a ministry that will be able or that will have the will to influence effectively science and technology in government.
As I interpret the legislation before the House, and notwithstanding the formation of the inter-council co-ordinating committee, the general thrust is substantially altered from that proposed by the two former ministers who held this portfolio since my arrival in Ottawa in 1972, and is more in keeping with the policies enunciated by this minister's immediate predecessor. If subsequent events confirm my impression that the present minister will be a toothless adviser to the cabinet, we may well be seeing the dismantling of the ministry if not in name then in terms of its effectiveness. I believe that would be tragic because I believe there is need for a positive, dynamic leadership on questions of science and technology. In my view the legislation does not provide the minister with such a mandate, and the prospects for the continuance of a fragmented approach to research and development in my view would persist in Canada.
The second question that is critical to the future of research and development is the government's medium and long term financial commitment. This has been covered by many other speakers during the debate today, Mr. Speaker. I want to indicate that in the past I have emphasized the necessity not only for medium financing, which is essential to bring the scientific community up to the standards we have known in the past, but also the necessity for a long term financial commitment on the part of the government. In my view this legislation is irrelevant unless that type of commitment is made.
All sorts of information has been brought to the attention of the minister and was referred to in the debate today. I would simply refer to additional information which was presented to parliamentarians in December when the research community visited Ottawa and met with members of parliament. I have no intention of reading their entire material into the record, but I should like to quote one or two points as follows:
In order to foster a healthy productivity and to encourage the innovative elements in Canadian research a measure of predictability must be incorporated in the budgeting of the granting councils. This is crucial, especially since two of them give three-year grants to particularly stable and established researchers and projects; thus any unexpected shortfalls in budgets result in a catastrophic compression of resources available for the new or annual renewal grants normally sought by our younger, developing investigators, or by those who seek to launch any new research projects.
Along with the need for a stable long-range financial commitment, Canadian research awaits a national science and research policy, including the long-sought modification of the NRC and Canada Council.
As one reviews the briefs and evidence submitted by the scientific community, it becomes abundantly clear that the government must make a financial commitment which will restore the strength of our scientific community to the level of the 1960's. The government must make long-term financial

December 13, 1976
Scientific Activities of Government
commitments which will allow the scientific community to arrange its priorities and establish that research base to which we can look forward in future.
My third point, which is most pertinent and has been mentioned by people involved in research, is that we must know the government's science and research policy for the future. This is absolutely essential. The scientific community, when we met with them in the first part of December mentioned some aspects which it is essential the government should enunciate. They include, for example, the government's concept of or commitment to maintaining research capability; its concept of minimum capabilities to be maintained in each major field and the target date for meeting that capability; the elements of economic and social goals of the government which would assist research communities in assessing and planning research and training priorities; and methods proposed for routine consultation within the research community.
In this regard I have been deeply shocked because, although there are excellent personnel on some of the granting councils, we do not yet have necessary feedback from the scientific community actually in the field and doing day to day research. I am impressed by the lack of input and disturbed because the minister does not have that type of dialogue at his disposal, dialogue which would be most helpful in assessing the work of the research community and the direction of future research in Canada.
In conclusion let me say that the reorganization of scientific endeavours as proposed by this bill raises far more questions than it answers. I am concerned because the bill does not define the future role of the Minister of State for Science and Technology, a role which could be most important. I say to the minister that this bill gives him no mandate, and therefore I am greatly apprehensive about the future of his particular ministry. In addition, the bill makes no medium and long-term financial commitment for ensuring the stability of the scientific community. As I said previously, it does not define the science policy of Canada. Certainly, the last three ingredients are absolutely essential if the legislation is to have any meaning and reorganize effectively scientific activities.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION (SCIENTIFIC ACTIVITIES) ACT, 1976 MEASURE RESPECTING ORGANIZATION OF CERTAIN SCIENTIFIC ACTIVITIES OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad for the opportunity to participate in the debate on Bill C-26, dealing with the reorganization of granting councils. It is not a bill dealing with science policy, the reorganization of the Ministry of State for Science and Technology, industrial strategy, or any of the other subjects to which various hon. members alluded today.
This reorganization of the granting councils provides us with an excellent opportunity to profit by our experience with such organizations as the National Research Council, the Canada Council, the Science Council of Canada and others which have

operated effectively in the past and in most cases performed their functions admirably according to their mandates.
Over the years, however, there has been a continuous evolution taking place and there is now a different perception of present and future needs to be fulfilled by such councils. They will be able, under this new structuring, to pursue more effectively the objective of a science policy which supports the planned use of science in order to achieve or further national goals.
We now have an opportunity to re-assess the direction in which science is leading us. We can plan more positively a second direction which will be of the greatest possible benefit to Canadians. My main concern is that, when the government is deciding on the make-up of the councils, the scientific community should have a significant input into the decisionmaking process so that there will be a just reflection of the various component disciplines which make up the spectrum of science, as well as a high level of expertise among members of the councils and geographical representation. I wish to say a few words about each of the proposed councils in turn.
The National Research Council has a well-deserved reputation for excellence both in Canada and abroad. NRC has made major contributions to scientific knowledge in the past and continues to focus its attention on problems with which we will be faced in the future such as, for example, alternative energy forms. That type of activity will continue, and I sincerely hope that the proposed reorganization will not be seen by NRC personnel as a downgrading of their role or as suggesting that their work until now has been anything short of excellent. Although restricting its work to the laboratories, the National Research Council will continue to play an important national role in the conduct of pure research as well as specific mission-oriented projects which have as their goal the solution to particular national problems.
The reorganization of the Medical Research Council will be minimal, merely providing for an expanded field of responsibility, namely, the public health field. Under its present mandate the Medical Research Council supports pure, applied, and clinical research in the health sciences. The expansion of its mandate to cover the whole area of health sciences is a logical progression which will enable the council to coordinate research among the different disciplines involved in that field. The change to allow the MRC to support public health research will not necessarily result in increased expenditures at this time, as from time to time priorities can be adjusted to reflect changing needs in the health sciences.
The need for a strong research capability in the social sciences may not be as apparent as that for medical research, which most people will agree is very important, or scientific research which can be translated into dollars earned and an expanded economy, but it is clearly an area which deserves much more support than it has received in the past. As the late John J. Duetsch told the National Social Science conference in November, 1975:
The human condition is to make choices with certain degrees of freedom but under various constraints. It is the role of the social scientists to enlarge the
December 13, 1976

degrees of freedom for all who must make choices, the politicians and the citizens, by exploring new options or different ways of reaching objectives and with varying benefits and costs. In order to do this social scientists have the responsibility to increase their knowledge of the issues and of the phenomena with which they deal. They have a responsibility to reduce the babble of confusing voices and to narrow the ranges of uncertainty by means of rational analysis and research.
We need sound social science research in order to have that fundamental self-knowledge without which sound social policies cannot be developed. Increasingly the social sciences are becoming essential to the successful translation of the pure sciences into practice. The social implications of modern technology cannot be ignored, and for proof we have only to look to the nuclear energy debate and the problems associated with the proposed northern oil and gas pipeline. The study of the social sciences is not a luxury which we can do without. The decision to divorce this research function from the Canada Council and establish a separate social sciences and humanities research council, with status equal to that of the other councils, demonstrates the recognition by the government of the important and useful work now being done by those studying social behaviour, and testifies to its enhanced importance in the future. The decision to increase the membership on the Science Council of Canada from 25 to 30 in order to make room for more social scientists is further evidence of this trend.
The Science Council is being given a new mandate which will involve educating the Canadian people about significant areas of science which will affect our way of life in the future. This has already been started, as demonstrated by, for example, the Science Council report on "Canada's Energy Opportunities". I feel that this role should be performed by a body such as the Science Council which is, in effect, at arm's length from the government, connected to it but not a part of it. Increasingly the Ministry of State for Science and Technology has been taking over some of the original responsibilities of the Science Council, and therefore this bill will remove some of the overlapping of responsibilities which have developed. I look forward to a Science Council which keeps in close contact with parliament so as to best fulfill its new role.
With regard to the Defence Research Board, this legislation reflects what is actually a fait accompli. My only criticism of the relationship of the DRB with the government is that I would prefer to see R&D being responsible at a higher level within the Department of National Defence. R&D reports to the chief, research and development, in the department. He, along with the chiefs of engineering and maintenance and of supply reports to the assistant deputy minister (materiel). This situation does not do justice to the important role research and development play in satisfying Canada's defence requirements. In the Department of Agriculture, there is an ADM responsible solely for research. It should be that way also in the Department of National Defence. Certainly this has been a cause of dissatisfaction and lowered morale among those working in the defence research establishments.
Scientific Activities of Government
The transfer of responsibility for Canadian Patents and Development Limited from the National Research Council to the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce is to be applauded, as it demonstrates recognition of the fact that the best technology in the world is of no practical use unless it can be translated into practice and become marketable. Because Industry, Trade and Commerce has an intimate knowledge of Canadian industry as well as contacts throughout the world which will facilitate the marketing of technology developed in Canada, this transfer is, again, extremely logical and praiseworthy, and I will be expecting an increased number of CP and DL patents being reduced to practice in industry as a result of ITC's involvement.
I am happy to give my support to Bill C-26 and look forward to the benefits for Canadian science which will be the result of its implementation.
I would now like to address a few remarks to the questions raised in this debate. This bill is in essence trying to build on the best tradition of the past. It is an evolutionary approach with a minimum of bureaucracy.
The opposition, primarily the Progressive Conservatives, have been trying to saddle this bill with everything having anything at all to do with science. This has been completely unrealistic. They are trying to say it should be responsible for industrial strategy, that it should be dealing with funding. Funding is a budgetary item and comes in, either in the blue book of estimates or in budget bills. It would not be encompassed at all in Bill C-26.
Bill C-26 is just one portion of the science problem area. It is an organization one relating primarily to university funding and allows universities to reassess their contribution in relation to national goals.
There has been talk of a government science policy from the opposition. There is no single science policy per se. This bill is part of an administrative framework for the various policies involved in a science strategy.
A total science policy takes on several forms. There is a policy for energy R&D. There is one being evolved for food R&D, one for space R&D which is primarily in the communications technology area, as well as an oceans policy. All these policies in these various areas are part of a total science policy. There is no one single all encompassing science policy.
Several comments have been made about the inter-council co-ordinating committee, the ICCC. Several comments which were made are very misleading. First, this committee, as it is proposed, is made up of the secretary of MOSST plus the three presidents of the three granting councils-the National Science and Engineering Research Council, the Medical Research Council and the Social Sciences Humanities Research Council. Others can be invited to meetings in connection with the subject under discussion, but basically the ICCC is a committee of four people. Therefore there is a small efficient group which can deal with the funding applications of borderline cases with respect to the areas of jurisdiction they fall into, and not a large layer of bureaucracy as stated by the

December 13, 1976
Scientific Activities of Government
hon. member for Halton-Wentworth (Mr. Kempling) and the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk).
The criticism that funding is suffering because of so much being spent on administration is another comment that is not valid. NRC spends roughly 2 per cent of its budget on administration for operating expenses. This level of the past is the same level that will be used in the future. Surely that is not an overly high level of spending for administration.
The hon. member for Athabasca criticized the proposal for the secretary of MOSST being the chairman of the ICCC. He was concerned about scientists being on the committee and not bureaucrats. First of all, there will be scientists on the ICCC. The president of the National Research Council and the president of the Medical Research Council are scientists. They have outstanding records of accomplishments. I am sure this past tradition will be continued with the appointments of the new presidents of the granting councils.
The secretary of MOSST is the best possible person to be the chairman of the ICCC. He has first hand knowledge of all R & D going on in the country, whether it be in government, university or industry. In government this includes not only the work in the National Research Council laboratories, but all departments involved in R & D Agriculture; Energy, Mines and Resources; Communications; Environment and Fisheries; National Health and Welfare, and CIDA.
The secretary of MOSST is in frequent contact with the Science Council, the Royal Society of Canada and SCITEC. As such, he is in an unusual and unique position. There is virtually no other person in this country who is so involved with all aspects of science and technology and its funding, hence my strong support for his being the chairman of the ICCC.
The hon. member for Halton-Wentworth says that perhaps MOSST is going out of business. The hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) says it should go out, that it is useless. Rubbish, I say. It is essential that we have planning and priority setting in the area of the spectrum of science and technology. If MOSST were disbanded, the work would have to be done elsewhere. It must be done; the question is where and how.
The opposition want instant answers and instant solutions. That is not only unrealistic, it is an injustice being perpetrated on the ignorance of the public by the PC's. It is typical of the PC's. There was an understanding with the opposition parties that only one day was needed for second reading of Bill C-26. The NDP and Creditiste have kept their word; the Tories, no. They do not really care about science and technology or the country. They only care about power, and obstructing any progress in this House.
Some hon. Members; Hear, hear!

The voices in which they discuss their discipline are so obscure that often the public cannot understand them and often, I think, they cannot understand one another. This is a serious indictment to make of social scientists and it is time scientists generally cleared up the nature of their language.
There is absolutely no reason why medicine, science, or any of the disciplines, including my own in law, should not be able to address the issues or matters they are undertaking on behalf of all of us in plain language, language which is easily understood. I have often wondered whether scientists sometimes prefer to be obscure simply as a tactic to keep their own domain untroubled by any public interest. This is an indictment I have made of them in their presence. It is really a plea for plain language.
As I have said, the bill has been a long time aborning. Of course the overhaul which is contained in Bill C-26 really has its origins in Senator Lamontagne's committee report. I should like to take a minute now to discuss what I think are a couple of the implications. Other members have drawn attention to their particular pets. Mine happens to be the Canada Council and, whether the hon. member for Wellington likes it or not, it is time we discussed funding and the implications of the spin-off from the Canada Council. As I understand it, there will be the same public servants and perhaps new officers, but

very little addition to the staff. I have personally no serious objection to this.
I,	and many others, have received representations in increasing numbers about the serious shortfall in funding for many of the artistic components, for instance, the various orchestras across the country. We are told by postcard, letter and telegram that the Treasury Board is proposing to keep budgetary increases in 1977 to within some 5 per cent, and this raises serious implications. As I understand Bill C-26, it is not a budget bill, as the hon. member for Wellington said, but it is a bill setting out the way in which the pie is to be sliced, so I do not expect to be taken to task by the Chair or anyone else for raising here the implications of the fact that there will, as I understand it, be very little more money despite the fact that the new councils are to be set up.
The other thing I should like to say is that I am troubled by the concept that just within a block or two of this building, probably not tonight, but certainly today or tomorrow it could happen-of course, the public is not intended to know, yet; these things are too obscure and complex for us to comprehend and therefore the meetings are behind closed doors-that there will be a further erosion, as 1 see it-I hope I am proved wrong and I will be delighted to apologise if I am proved wrong-of the national underpinning of post-secondary education by a mere transfer of tax points from the national government to the provinces. I am not making this comment just because I happen to come from one of the smaller, have-not, provinces. I am an unreconstructed Corryire, believing, like J. A. Corry, that there is a federal obligation based very soundly in the constitution, although like all constitutions perhaps it was not as clearly stated in 1867 as we would wish in 1976. However, any look at the Blue Book will show the dollar involvement of the national government in post-secondary education or, for that matter, in education in general.
Public people down through the ages, since this country was founded, have been using all kinds of euphemisms for education. We have set up councils of ministers of education for the provinces although, as I understand it, there is no federal presence there. There is, perhaps, an observer, but certainly no federal minister attends. At any rate, not since the days of the Pearson government have we had under the Prime Minister's own sponsorship an advisory group dealing with post-secondary education at the ministerial level. It is my understanding that a middle-rank official is now undertaking this advisory role for the Department of the Secretary of State.
I believe national responsibility for post-secondary education is one of the aspects of what we might call the new federalism, or the new constitutional arrangements which might be necessary if, as we all devoutly hope, we are to have new arrangements in order to persuade one of our provinces at least to stay within the Canadian family. It is time for those of us who believe this-and I do not believe it is a particularly partisan view-who believe in the national responsibility of postsecondary education, to stand up. For example, it seems to me I read the other day a speech by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) to the Canadian Tax Foundation in which he said
Scientific Activities of Government the federal government wanted to sit at the table, that is, the table of education. Certainly I think that is justified.
It seems to me almost incomprehensible, in a country of two official languages that spends massive federal funding on post-secondary education, that there is still no possibility, I understand at least up to this point, for the federal government to require any qualification for university entrance. It seems to me totally wrong, for example, that any university in this country would not as a matter of course expect facility in the French language and in the English language for university entrance. I do not care if a student is going to be a doctor or is going to pursue courses of a more general nature not in a particular discipline; this in 1976 is, it seems to me, not an outrageous request.
I do not think we should make such a request on the basis of money, although I suppose money can tell a tale and can also be a persuasive element. In other words, the national government has a responsibility in post-secondary education, and there follows from it certain requirements for national dollars which universities should accept as a matter of course in participating in the citizenship of this country. Perhaps some people would think this is a simple-minded suggestion. I hope not, but to me it is a rather obvious one.
I have not seen very much press on Bill C-26, so I hope that the minister, with his usual modesty, will not be overly sensitive at that fact. Perhaps my research on Bill C-26 is not very good, or perhaps the reason is that this bill has been promised for so long. Nevertheless I did find an interesting editorial in the Montreal Gazette a week ago which explained the bill and suggested that the new councils might support research, first of all, into discovering why it has taken the government so long to get to the place we have arrived at today. This might be a very interesting research project for an M.A. thesis. After all, it has taken three years to bring about something that the government decided to do that many years ago. Perhaps that says something about the arrangements we have here in parliament.
I do feel some sympathy with the government. I do not know whether this bill has been prepared for some time and the government just keeps changing the date each year, or changing it as ministers change. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has not yet changed, though that is an inevitable consequence and will indeed happen. Anyway, perhaps it would be a good idea to have a research paper into why a rather modest proposal involving no extra expenditure should take so long to get to this stage.
If I may just spend a few further minutes, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say something further. I agree that the clock situation does make things difficult. I keep looking at the clock, and although I think I have spoken for a long time, I find I really have not.

speechtext:
It is still only eight o'clock. The Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Guay) reminds me that my speech is of such a high degree of intelligence that he thinks it is going more quickly than I do. In any event, may I refer to the Canada Council part of the bill for a moment.
I wonder whether the hon. member for Wellington, or whoever on the government side is going to make the next speech, would like to reflect on the fact that it has been, after all, some 25 years since the Massey report which ultimately was responsible for setting up the Canada Council. Perhaps it would be a fairly good time for the government to consider taking another look at the question. I am not persuaded that it is a good idea to have another royal commission. I am rather cynical about contemporary royal commissions. I think the public is commissioned, task forced, and researched to death. Surely the advisers to the government could assemble themselves into a group to take a look at the Canada Council, at where it has been, and what contribution it has made to the reinforcement of the arts in our country.
Some of us are old enough to remember the days before the Canada Council. If anyone wants an example of what it was like before the Canada Council was set up, they should look at the operating budgets of some of the great national orchestras of our country. They should look at the number of artists, authors, poets and so on and see what these creative people have been doing. What I am really saying is that perhaps it is time for a stocktaking of the last 25 years; then, if it is not too dangerous an idea, perhaps we should then look ahead. It is my understanding that if the present day budget projections are accurate, many of the creative and artistic aspects of Canadian life will be in very great jeopardy, not only in the decade ahead but during the next four or five years.
It may be that such a look, Mr. Speaker, could devise a system for making more generous tax arrangements so that the private sector could participate more actively in this field. I, as the representative of a small province, have been an enthusiastic supporter in general terms of state intervention. People get knee jerky about state intervention, but the intervention of the state is really nothing very different from the intervention of the prince in earlier days, and personally I am more comfortable with the state and the Canada Council than I am with the patronage of princes. Perhaps we should look not only at the catalogue of achievements of the Canada Council but also at some projections as to where what we call the humanities and the artistic aspects of our life are going to be in the next few years.
I think that is about all that hon. members will want to hear from me on this topic. I should like, at some time or other, to have an opportunity to discuss, in terms that will not offend the hon. member for Wellington as to relevance, the whole subject of the student in university and what I see as the mean spirited view-and in saying that I set myself up to be shot down-on the part of many provincial governments today in that there is a toll at our provincial gate, a separation possibly in domestic terms of those who come from New Brunswick

and Nova Scotia to attend some of the great institutions of Ontario and Quebec.
Certainly there is a toll at the gate of Canada for those who seek to come to these institutions to study. I think this is a mean-spirited concept, and I regret to see it is most manifest in the two richest provinces in our country. There are national implications to having higher fees for foreign students. I regret the fact that Canada, the country we serve, has had little to say about this, although the higher fees for foreign students obviously affects the international posture of this country.
I think for example of the Prime Minister, who obviously when he was at the Sorbonne did not pay an extra fee because he was a Canadian student, and nor did he presumably when he went to Harvard. There are many members who have had similar experiences and, of course, there are hundreds of thousands of people around the world who have benefited from the generosity of respective national states. I believe very firmly that this sort of "scholars for dollars," surely one of the most demeaning slogans of the last two or three years, could have serious implications for Canada.
I hope it never happens within our own country, although it obviously happens with quotas. There are quotas-so many New Brunswick people can go here and so many Prince Edward Island people can go there. Canada was not founded on quotas. Some of our great international universities which speak really to the world surely would never have gained such undoubted reputations if they had a sliding scale that affects people from all over the world.
The hon. member for Wellington and others may suggest that I am well beyond the scope of a second reading debate, but this includes the Canadian Committee on Financing University Research, and that is the hook on which I am hanging this plea. Really this is a plea that the provinces in this country not take what I think is a retrograde step of having different requirements in money terms for people who come from outside Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Tuesday, December 7, as reported in Hansard at page 1730,1 put this question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau):
In light of the discussions the Prime Minister and his colleagues had yesterday with representatives of the National Council of Women and in view of the many ways in which pension plans under the aegis of the government discriminate against women, will the government consider establishing a review of all pension
Adjournment Debate
plans that come under the responsibility of the government with a view to ending discrimination against women?
I went on to give four examples. The first point I want to make in raising the question again tonight is that I directed my question to the Prime Minister because I am concerned not just about something in one department, but about something that raises its ugly head in a number of departments. However, because the subject was pensions the Prime Minister passed the question back to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde). I see by the process of elimination it is his parliamentary secretary who will be answering me tonight.
Although I gave four examples of discrimination against women so far as pensions are concerned, and I will come back to those examples in a moment, the key portion of the reply of the Minister of National Health and Welfare was in these words:
-I want to deny that allegation most vigorously. What the hon. member sees as discrimination is not directed against one sex in particular; it is merely a matter of dealing differently with people according to the conditions in which they find themselves, be they male or female. That has nothing to do with the status of women as such.
I hope the parliamentary secretary will not give us the same line tonight that his minister gave us the other day. What the minister tried to say was that perhaps women are not getting pension equality with men but it is not because they are women but because they are not in the labour market and therefore do not qualify for the pension plan, or for a number of other reasons. What I sought through my question the other day was a review with a particular interest. I asked that all pension plans be looked at to determine whether there is discrimination against women and whether something can be done about it.
Let us take a few of the examples. I cited the Canada Pension Plan which does not cover housewives. The minister says that is not discrimination against them because they are women; they are just denied it because they are not in the labour market. Put any name you want on it, the largest group of people who are left out of the Canada Pension Plan is women. Mostly they are housewives. I suggest that no matter what appellation you give it, that is discrimination.
Next I go on to the spouse's allowance. The spouse's allowance is set up nominally on an equal basis, male or female, but in terms of statistics the persons who suffer the most because they cannot qualify for a pension under the spouse's allowance are spinsters and widows between the ages of 60 and 65. Statistics already show that the persons who, for the most part, are cut off the spouse's allowance before they are 65, are women whose older husbands have died.
I move on to veterans' pensions. There again there is discrimination which the minister might say is not because of the fact that they are women but because they are widows. Mr. Speaker, it is the same thing. I note in particular that the widow of a veteran who received a 48 per cent pension or more gets the full widow's pension, but the widow of a veteran whose pension was less than 48 per cent does not get a pension

December 13, 1976
Adjournment Debate
as a right but must fall back on the war veteran's allowance. So the persons who are discriminated against most in terms of pensions that come under the Department of Veterans Affairs are, in my view, women.
Then there is the largest group of all, women who survived their husbands and, at best, get a 50 per cent pension. This applies, I admit, not just in pensions that come under the government, but it applies across the board. There are some 60 per cent pensions but, for the most part, the pension is 50 per cent. Here you have a man and wife who live and work together. They produce a certain estate, certain pension rights. Let us say they both live until the breadwinner goes on pension, and that pension is a certain amount. If the man dies first, the woman's pension is 50 per cent; if the woman dies first, the surviving husband's pension is 100 per cent. No matter how thin you slice it, no matter how you describe it, that is discrimination against women.
This government did not create it; it is something we have inherited after decades of a double standard.

subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION AGAINST WOMEN IN PENSION PLANS-REQUEST FOR REVIEW
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me first repeat what the minister previously stated in response to this question. He said that the hon. member sees sex discrimination where in fact none exists. I would say the hon. member has probably cleared some of that up this evening. He agrees that most of these plans are set up on the basis of equality to each sex. It is just that more of one sex get caught in some of these problems.
I would like to deal first with the question of the spouse's allowance.
The spouse's allowance was introduced to provide additional income in situations where a couple is living on a single pension and the pensioner's spouse is between 60 and 65 years of age. The hon. member may not agree with the provisions of the spouse's allowance, but nonetheless there is no discrimination in that the same benefits are provided to male and female alike. The hon. member should not try to confuse the public on this point, and I think he has cleared it up at this stage.
With respect to the Canada Pension Plan, I point out that the plan was amended in 1975 to provide equal treatment for women and men. As this House knows, the government also intends to introduce in this session two further amendments to the plan to give recognition to the economic contribution of both partners in a marriage.

The first amendment will propose that pension credits earned by spouses during marriage may be divided equally between them if the marriage is dissolved. The second provision will enable any Canada Pension Plan contributor who leaves the labour force to raise children under age seven to drop out those months of low or zero earnings in the calculation of pension entitlement.
The hon. member mentioned allowances for widows and widowers of public servants. It should be noted that here too the formula for benefits is identical whether the surviving spouse is male or female, and therefore it cannot be construed to be discriminatory.
The hon. member spoke of benefits paid to surviving spouses of veterans and would have us believe that benefits are denied to veterans' widows. This is simply not the case. Pensions are provided on the same basis to both sexes. Again, the hon. member may disagree with the terms of the pension, but he cannot say that it is on the basis of sex discrimination that he disagrees.
I would also like to take this opportunity to mention that Bill C-25, the Canadian human rights legislation, proscribes discrimination in pensions and fringe benefits in all establishments under federal jurisdiction. As the hon. member is no doubt aware, a wide range of establishments come under provincial rather than federal jurisdiction. For this reason during the last year and a half a federal-provincial committee has been examining how best to eliminate sex discrimination in pensions and benefits. The federal government has made provision within its own statutes relating to pensions to ensure equitable treatment for women and men, and Bill C-25 extends such provisions to all establishments under federal jurisdiction.
It should be noted that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) recently announced that an inter-departmental committee has been engaged in a comprehensive review of the whole area of pensions of Canadians with a view to assessing whether any significant changes in policy should be considered. This certainly would include any possible sex discrimination.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 24, 1976, I asked the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) a question with respect to the basis upon which the government was avoiding the call by the Auditor General of Canada for the appointment of a chief financial
December 13, 1976

officer. My question was based on the fact that in a previous statement the minister had said that such an appointment could possibly challenge the whole structure of parliamentary responsibility, ministerial responsibility to parliament, and the rights of members of this House. Quite frankly, there must be a better reason than that because that reason has no force or validity whatsoever, in my respectful opinion, and I say to my colleagues in this House that if there was a challenge to hon. members of this House, I would be the first one to raise the matter.
I presumed in the question that the financial officer would be basically dealing with senior levels of the public service on accounting and financial matters of the ministry. I presumed his annual report would be tabled in parliament in the normal course. I further presumed that the work of the Public Accounts Committee would be facilitated because many of the things which the Auditor General would normally deal with would be caught at the outset, and therefore the work would be lighter. The minister tended to agree with me, but still he evaded the point, and although he has moved in the direction of appointing departmental financial officers, the main thrust of the report of the Auditor General is still clouded by some spurious desire for a royal commission, which is really unnecessary in view of the work that was done by the Auditor General.
The problem is a serious one. In his report the Auditor General said this:
Based on the study of the systems of departments, agencies and Crown Corporations audited by the Auditor General, financial management and control in the Government of Canada is grossly inadequate.
Not just inadequate, but grossly inadequate.
Furthermore, it is likely to remain so until the Government takes a strong, appropriate and effective measure to rectify this critically serious situation.
Those are the strongest words which have ever been used by the Auditor General, not with respect to an isolated instance or a series of them, but with respect to a course of conduct. He has said that the system is wrong. He also said that the Government of Canada cannot produce accurate accounts of its spending.
What is going on when the Auditor General tells us that this vast bureaucracy is so fumble-fingered with the money it holds in trust and spends on our behalf that he is not sure how much is being wasted, how much is non productive, and that he cannot assure us that fraud has not been committed? Given the dimensions of the problem, which Treasury Board officials concede, what is to be done?
The Auditor General, supported by his independent advisory committee consisting of accountants from Canada's top firms, wants a comptroller general of Canada and wants the government to make sure that whoever fills this position comes from an outstanding financial background.
This is a position similar to that of the comptroller of a company, assuming Treasury Board's responsibility in this
Adjournment Debate
field, and reporting as a deputy minister to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras), and supported by a senior financial officer in each department to advise the deputy head. That first little step has now been taken.
So that no one could sit on him, the departmental financial officer would either rank equal or above everyone but the deputy minister, or he could not do his job. This the government has failed to see, or has refused to see the significance of the recommendations. Take your pick-except maybe the eyes are opening slightly. I hope they will open all the way. In fact the Treasury Board's response has been extremely negative where the key recommendation of the Auditor General's report are concerned.
I will not go into the complex push and pull between the Auditor General and the President of the Treasury Board. As I see it, the response of Treasury Board has been threefold. First, it has agreed to tinker extensively with the existing system following some of the secondary recommendations of the Auditor General. Second, it has rejected as constitutionally inappropriate the heart of the Auditor General's report-the need for a comptroller general-but now it has moved toward having financial officers in the departments. This is something new, and I hope it is the first of many steps to be taken by the government. I urge it to do so. Third, it has appointed a royal commission composed of career public servants who probably will lobby for the status quo, on the one hand, and accountants who will probably agree with their colleagues on the other. I think the government has really said, "Yes, we agree some horses have run away, but we think it would be inappropriate to close the barn door. However, we will repaint it."
The royal commission is a patent attempt to forestall any criticisms the Auditor General might make before the Public Accounts Committee or in the next year's report. No doubt it is also designed, just in case the same diagnosis is made again, to delay further serious criticism or action until after the next federal election. For Heaven's sakes-let us forget such an evasion and get on with implementing the Auditor General's recommendation. Let me state unequivocally that such a move by the government to create that office would have the support of our party.
We utterly reject this phony constitutional argument which is being tried on the people of Canada. More than that, the people of Canada reject it as well. I am sure that they regard the cynicism behind this move as simply breathtaking, as I do.
I fail to see where the constitutional responsibility of departmental officials, their ministers or ministry to the House of Commons, is interfered with by the Auditor General's recommendations. There is no reason why that Auditor General's report ought not to be implemented in the fullest. It is one of the finest reports ever brought to this House by someone who has weighed his words like a diplomat, with great care, and who in subdued language has painted a picture which has brought the Canadian taxpayer to despair. The government owes a duty to the Canadian taxpayer to lift that burden of despair and to ensure some recommendation is implemented, providing something new in terms of the public accounts of

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of my colleague, the hon. Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Trudel) I am pleased to make a brief reply to the important question which has been raised this evening by the House leader of the Official Opposition, the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker).
The hon. member will of course recall the forthright way in which the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) responded to his inquiry on November 24 with reference to the recommendation of the Auditor General for a chief financial officer of the government. The minister said that there could be patterns where this could be done. He went on to say that he found a certain appeal and attraction for the proposition, so much so that he wanted to be quite sure about those other matters. Those other matters to which he referred concerned ministerial responsibility, the structure of parliament, and the rights of members. All these questions must be considered. As the President of the Treasury Board said, all these questions have to be answered. In the meantime there are many things we are going to do. We are not going to wait.
Therefore when the hon. member opposite suggests that there has been a negative response, he is not being fair to the President of the Treasury Board. The government has always approached positively the reports of the Auditor General. For example, I remind the House again that when the Auditor General presented his report one year ago, he proposed 34 recommendations. The former president of the treasury board who is now Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien) accepted 32 of those recommendations.

subtopic: TRANSPORT-USE OF FOREIGN NAVAL ARCHITECTS TO DESIGN EAST COAST FERRY REPLACEMENTS
TRANSPORT-USE OF FOREIGN NAVAL ARCHITECTS TO DESIGN EAST COAST FERRY REPLACEMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) of October 22 expressed concern about the government's ship construction program and contained a criticism about its ship chartering policy. This is the matter to which I address my remarks this evening.
In a brief presented to the government on April 26 of this year, the Canadian Shipbuilding and Ship Repairing Association submitted an elaborate and detailed plan to keep the Canadian shipbuilding industry afloat. The government has largely ignored such plan. Among other things, the industry took exception, with just cause, to the present government policy of chartering foreign ships to provide ferry services to Canada. This policy, apparently to be continued indefinitely in future, is all the more objectionable since there are expert technology, manpower and slipways in this country and we are ready at any time to design and lay down keels to meet Canadian requirements. Moreover, our shipyards need the contracts. The Abegweit, for example, is due to be replaced by a ship designed by a Danish firm or built in Scandinavian yards. Possibly it will be both designed and built in Scandinavia, and chartered.
The ships serving the Sydney-Port Aux Basques route are now on charter from a Swedish firm and there seems to be no attempt to have them replaced by ships built in Canadian yards. One can only wonder why the government and the department seem to distrust Canadian expertise. Five of these ships are at present on the CN's east coast service. Such foreign ships are described in the trade as bare boat charters, which means, I assume, that basically the bottom is chartered but that the ship is crewed by Canadians. Whether such ships are refitted to meet Canadian safety standards is a matter at issue. In this connection may I quote part of the letter sent to the Minister of Transport by the Canadian Shipbuilding and Ship Repairing Association. It said in part:
. ..ships under bare-boat charter need only meet the 1960 Safety of Life at Sea ... IMCO requirements whereas the Canadian built ships are required to adhere to the 1974 SOLAS requirements which are much more stringent and entail greater building costs. Hence, the chartered ships have a cost advantage but are comparatively less safe than would the Canadian new buildings that must adhere to the 1974 SOLAS requirements.
The Shipping Association is of the view that this method of meeting the east coast shipping need, in addition to being comparatively less safe is likely to be not only more expensive over the long run, but will also mean that the expenditures are lost to Canadian shipyards and the Canadian economy. I have it on the best authority, and I hope that the parliamentary secretary who will be replying will carry this to the minister, that if the Department of Transport wants to continue in this way, at least one replacement ferry could be designed and built in Canada and put out to bare boat charter at no capital cost to the federal treasury and at a comparative figure. If it could be done for one, I suspect it could be done for others.
December 13, 1976

Another practice to which the industry takes exception is having designs vetted offshore by a foreign firm. We are almost back in the foreign agent business. Does the minister not trust our own native ship design competence? Elas he not seen what it can produce and set afloat, on Lake Huron for example, and in many other instances? Who is to get the final design contract? This is what has happened. The Canadian plans have been drawn and sent offshore to be vetted. However, who is to get the final design contract once these Canadian plans have been approved by the Danish consultants-the Canadian designer or the Danish designer-and who is to build the ferry? Has the minister really investigated this matter carefully and has he had it costed in terms of the Canadian economy, the Canadian industry, and of Canadian ability to meet our own needs in the future in this area?
We are going to need a good many sturdy patrol ships designed for Canadian waters, preferably by Canadians, to meet our fisheries patrol needs. Has the minister taken this into account in refusing to keep our shipyards alive until Fisheries makes up its mind as to when it is going to build its patrol vessels?
Our shipyards are laying men off by the tens and by the hundreds. They will not be around to build the fisheries patrol vessels nor the naval patrol vessels needed to strengthen our patrol facilities with the approaching day of the 200 mile limit. When will the minister see this? Why is he not taking action now? Why is he not trusting Canadian industry?

subtopic: TRANSPORT-USE OF FOREIGN NAVAL ARCHITECTS TO DESIGN EAST COAST FERRY REPLACEMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Roy), I am pleased to reply to the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro), regarding the use by the Department of Transport of foreign naval architects to design east coast ferries, which could in the future serve as replacements for such east coast ferries as the Abegweit,
Adjournment Debate
Nautica, Atlantic and Nordica vessels, and I am pleased to provide the following information.
In March, 1975, the contract for the design of a vessel, suitable for ferry service to the east coast, was awarded through competitive tender to Case Existological Laboratories Limited (CELL) of Victoria, B.C. The hon. member will understand that because of the rapid advances in the design of ferries of this type which have been made in Europe in recent years, the design contract provided for the association of the Canadian naval architect, CELL, with a European designer.
He will also understand the advantages which Canada would derive from such an association, first, the promotion and development of Canadian expertise in ferry design and, second, the development of the best and most economical design, one which would incorporate the latest advances in technology and concept.
Upon completion of the preliminary design phase, in view of the indefinite timing of construction of these ferry vessels, the Department of Transport requested the Department of Supply and Services on April 15, 1976 to initiate action which would terminate the contract with CELL-Case Existological Laboratories Limited. The Department of Supply and Services is processing the termination of the contract at the present time.
I am pleased to add, in summary, that on October 13, 1976, the Department of Transport confirmed that the preliminary design data provided by CELL would be acceptable as base documentation should it be decided at a later date to proceed with the project to construct new ferry vessels. I know the hon. gentleman will greet this news with Christian cheer and positive joy, qualities which so often reside in his charitable heart.
